,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   vi  PREFACE  Hints on Chemistry Practicals is over two   decades in the making. The  information contained in this book is a product of over 2o years of classroom  interactions with students. It is intentionally and explicitly written to make  chemistry learning enjoyable. There is a place for every student. Even i f you have  serious foundation problem, an aspect titled: ‘ Chemistry for Beginners’   has  been added to address that. Above all, this book contains over 25 years of past  questions which include WAEC, NECO, JAMB and others.  Hints on Chemistry Practicals   touches virtually every aspect of chemistry via  practicals.  Quantitative and qualitative analyses have been thoroughly explained. They   have  been explained in a very simple language with various examples that will  enhance student’s understanding greatly   .  The various build up to quantitative analysis such as acid, base and salt, mole  concept, stoichiometry of reactions, calculations on Gas laws and water of  crystallization , PH and heat of reactions etc, have been well explained.  Electrode   potential, elect rolysis and redox reactions which are considered  problematic have   also be dealt with .   The calculation on titrations is detailed and  covers all the parts required in the various syllabi, including calculations on  redox and solubility.  The qualitative analy sis did not stop at tests for anions and cations. It went  further to address : identification of organic compounds, extractions of metals ,  solubility of salts in water, effect of heat on salts, rates of chemical reactions,  collections of gases, and much m ore . And if you have challenges with naming  and isomerism, a chapter has been added to address such problem.  This book is written in   simplicity   such that every science student can understand  it easily   even if he/she is a mediocre or below -   average studen t .   It is important to  say that Hints on Chemistry Practicals   is not written to provide a nswers to past  questions alone,   rather, to teach a student step by step and show him/her how to  apply the knowledge in solving problems.  Every science student, includi ng SS1   and   SS2, will find it very helpful particularly  the valency and how compounds are formed as well as so me basic knowledge of  chemistry such as Atomic structure , periodic table and calculations on moles.  It contains very many questions and answers t o past questions of WAEC, NECO  and JAMB besides other questions which are al so helpful to students  T here is no doub t, Hints on Chemistry Practicals stands out   as one of the best  piece on Chemistry ever written for   SSCE,GCE,NECO AND   JAMB.  This book is cert ainly an exceptional material. Enjoy it.  E.J. NWANKWO ⓒ 2023  Joe_sef222@yahoo.com

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   1  LET’S START WITH THE APPARATUS  To carry out tests on salts, the most important apparatus you will need is the test tubes. They are  safely kept with the test tubes racks. There are different types. The boiling test tubes ar e for tests  that requires boiling. The ignition test tubes are for tests that require heating.  To filter a mixture, you need a funnel and a filter paper. The filter paper is folded twice and  inserted inside the test tubes.  Always use a test tube   clamp   to hold test tubes while boiling or heating its content. And always  point the test tube in a slant position away from yourself and   your   colleagues.  To grind salts into powder in order to increase their surface area of reaction, you will need the  mortar an d pestle.  To put salts into the test tubes, you will the spatula or the deflagration spoon.  To add water to salts in a test tube you need the aspirator bottle….wash bottle. The dropping  pipette is essentially for adding drops of indicator during titration   experiments

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   2  What’s more?  Yes, the burette is for holding liquid solutions like acid during titration  The pipette is for measuring accurately a fixed volume of liquid solution like base during  titration. The common volume sizes are 20cm 3   or 25cm 3 .  Retort stand fitted with clamp is for holding the burette in a vertical position for ease of titration  A set up for evaporation is always done with an evaporating dish on water bath or sand bath  placed on a tripod stand. Wire gauze is usually pl aced on the tripod stand first to ensure uniform  heating.  The beakers are used to keep acids or bases before titration  Flasks are the containers where titration experiments are carried out. There are different types.  We have conical flask, round bottom fla sk and the flat bottom flask.  For accurate measurement of mass of salts, you need the chemical balance.  To pass   gas from one test to another solution or salt, you need a bubbler or delivery tube.  The bursen burner is always the heat source. And a brush use d for washing the test tubes

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   5  SAFETY PRECAUTIONS  Right now, I want to warn you seriously. The laboratory is not your playground. So whenever you are in a  chemistry laboratory, be very careful, particularly, when you are   carrying out experiments.  The most important thing to do actually is to adhere strictly to the instructions of your teacher. Safety  precautions are usually written on the walls of the laboratory.Do not break the rules.  Few safety rules to keep in mind.  Always wear   laboratory coats   and eye shields or   safety goggles .  When handling acids and bases, be very careful.   It is dangerous to add water to concentrated acids. Acids  should be added to water with stirring always.  Always use both hands to carry big rea gent bottles.  When heating, use test tubes holder for test tubes and crucible tongs for crucible.  Do not heat the contents of test tubes facing yourself or your colleagues  Do not taste, smell or touch unless you are told to do so.  More so, if you must smel l a gas, use your palm to fan the gas towards your nose.  Do not hold reagent bottle by the neck.  In case of any accident, report it to your teacher immediately! However, for fire incidents, use the fire  extinguisher.  Ensure you know the on a reagent bottle   before using its contents.  Always keep the laboratory neat and tidy. Replace all reagent bottles and other apparatus on the shelves  after use.  More so, do not handle electrical apparatus with wet hands. Always put the switch off before plugging in  or unpl ugging electrical apparatus.  When heating or boiling liquids, always shake the boiling - tube constantly to avoid spurting.

Volume of  pipette used   must   also be recorded but no account of experimental procedure must be  required. Allcalculations   must   be done in your answer book.  A   is a solution containing 12.0 g dm - 3   .   B   is a solution contain ing NaOH.  (a)   Put   A   into the burette and titrate it against 20.0 cm 3   or 25.0 cm 3   portions of   B  using methyl orange as indicator. Repeat the titration to obtain   consistent   titres. Tabulate  your burette readings and calculate the average volume of aci d   A   used.  The equation for the reaction involved in the titration is:  NaHSO 4(aq)   + NaOH (aq)   Na 2 SO 4(aq)   + H 2 O (l)  (b)   From your result and the information provided above, calculate:  ( i )   Concentration of   A   in   mol dm - 3 ;  ( ii )   Concentration of   B   in   mol dm - 3 ;  ( iii )   Mass of   Na +   formed in solution during titration  SAMPLE QUESTION ON QUANLITATIVE ANALYSIS  (WASSCE2014 )  2 . Credit will be given for strict adherence to the instructions, for observations precisely  recorded and accurate inferences. All test, observation and inferences   must be clearly  entered in your a nswer book, in   ink,   at the time they are made.  C   and   D   are in organic salts.   X   is a solution of an inorganic compound. Carry out the  following exercises on   C, Dand   X . Record your observation and identify any gas   (es)  evolved. State the conclusion drawn from the result of   each   test.  a)   Add about 5cm 3   of distilled water to   C   in a test tube and shake thoroughly.  (i)   Divide the resulting solution into two portions.  (ii)   Put about 2cm 3 of   X   into a separate test tube and add the first  portionof solution in   2(a) (i).  (iii)   To the portion of the resulting solution in   2(a) (i),   add few  drops of   BaCl 2   (aq)   followed by excess   dil. HCl.  b)   Add about   10cm 3   of distilled water to   D   in a boiling tube and  shakethoroughly.  (i)   To about 2cm 3   of the resulting solution in a test tube, add  NaOH   (aq )   in   drops   and then in excess.  (ii)   To another 2cm 3   portion of the resulting solution add few drops of  K 2 C r O 4(aq)

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   9  CURRENT WAEC   SYLLABUS ON QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS  No formal scheme of analysis is required.  (i) Characteristic tests of the following cations with   dilute NaOH (aq)   and  NH 3(aq);  NH 4 + ; Ca 2+ ; Pb 2+ ; Cu 2+ ; Fe 2+ ; Fe 3+ ; Al   3+ ; and Zn 2+  (ii) Confirmatory tests for the above   cations.  (iii) Characteristic reaction of   dilute HCl   on solids or aqueous solutions and  conc.H 2 SO 4   on solid samples of the following:  Cl -   , SO 3 2 -   ; CO 3 2 -   ;   NO 3 -   and SO 4 2 -  (iv) Confirmatory tests for the above anions  (v) Compara tive study of the halogens; displacement reactions.  (vi)   Characteristic tests for the following gases:  H 2 ; NH 3 ; CO 2 ; HCl and SO 2 .  (vii) Characteristic test tube reactions of the functional groups in the  following simple organic compound s:  Alkenes; alkanols; alkanoic acids,  sugars   (using Fehiling’s and Benedict’s solutions only);  starch (iodine test only) and  proteins  (using the Ninhydrin test, Xanthoporteic test, Biuret test and Millon’s test only).

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   10  QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS  AIM :   To identify theanions and the cations present in a given substance  INTRODUCTION  ELECTRODE : ANODE AND CATHODE  E lectrodes   are metallic conductors. They are of two types: ANODE and CATHODE.  The anode forms the positive electrode while the cathode is the negative electrode.  Graphite is the only non - metal which can be used as electrode because it can conduct electricity  like me tals  Notice that the   an ode   and   the   cath ode   ha ve something in common. They both   end with  ‘ ODE ’. This is because they are electrodes.  IONS : ANIONS AND CATIONS  During electrolysis,   the ion which goes to the anode (or   positive electrode ) are called   anode  ions or anions or negative ions.     Thus,   while the ANODE   is a   positive electrode ,the ANION is a   negative ION     ANIONS are also called non metallic ions.  Examples   of anions are   :   Cl -   , SO 3 2 -   ; CO 3 2 -   ;   NO 3 -   and SO 4 2 -  Similarly, the negative electrode or cathode will attract the   posive ions during electrolysis.  Thus, the positive ions are called   cathode ions or cations.  Thus,   while the CATHODE   is a   negative electrode ,the CATIONS are   negative ION S  CATIONS   are also called metallic ions.  Notice that the   an ode   and   the   cath ode   ha ve something in common. They both   end with   ‘ION’.  This is because they are IONS.  Examples   cations are   : NH 4 + ; Ca 2+ ; Pb 2+ ; Cu 2+ ; Fe 2+ ; Fe 3+ ; Al   3+ ; and Zn 2+

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   11  KIPP’S APPARATUS  C   = HCl   A   =H 2 S  C   +   B   A  HCl   +   FeS   FeCl 2   +   H 2 S  Kipp’s ap paratus is used for intermittent supply of any gas needed in the laboratory  If B = CaCO 3 , then A= CO 2  HCl   +   CaCO 3   Ca Cl 2   +   CO 2  Hint:  Anode and anion are   like husband and wife. They always go together but their charges are  different. While anode is positive   electrode , an anion is a negative ion.  Similarly, c athode and anion are also like husband and wife. They always go together but  their charges are oppos ite to each other. While cathode is   a   negative   electrode , a cation is a  positive ion.  Note:   Anode and cathode are conductors while anions and cations are ions.  ‘ ppt’   means precipitate   ‘ex’   means excess   ‘aq’   means aqueous   ‘dil’   means dilute,  ‘conc’   means concentrated   ‘s’   means solid   ‘l’   means liquid   ‘g’   means gas

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   12  COMPREHENSIVE STUDY ON GASES

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   13  INTRODUCTION TO GASES  During the tests for anions, some gases are always given off when certain  reagents are added to them.  Before going any further, it is very important to study these gases at this point.  Why?   This is because the gas evolved (or liberated or given off) helps us to  identify the anion present in a given substance  EXPLANATION  If you cannot identify CO 2   gas, how would you know the anion present is CO 3 2 -   ?  If you cannot identify SO 2   gas, how would   you know the anion present is SO 3 2 -   ?  Only a monkey can give birth to a monkey! Hahaha!!  This is why you should know the gases at this point  Once the gas is H 2 S, you would know the anion present is   a   sulphide ion ( S 2 -   )  The lime water will turn milky to show that CO 2   gas is liberated

The acidic gases are:   Cl 2 (g) , HCl (g),   NO 2 (g) , H 2 S (g)   , SO 2(g)   and CO 2(g)  - The neutral gases are:   O 2 (g)   , H 2 (g),   N 2 O   (g),   water vapour ( or H2O   (g)   )  -   NO 2 , Cl 2 , HCl, H 2 S and   NH 3   gases should be prepared in a fume chamber.   Why?  Because of their offensive smell or poisonous nature.  2.   Ammonia ( (NH 3 ) ) is the only alkaline gas.  This means, it is the   only gas   which turns red litmus paper blue.  3.   Ammonia gas gives dense white fumes with HCl .The   dense   white   fumes is  ammonium chloride  NH 3   + HCl   →   NH 4 Cl  4.   Chlorine gas [Cl 2 gas ] turns   bromine water yellow or orange.  It is a displacement reaction because   Cl 2(g)   displaces Br (g)   .  This   reaction   is a general characteristic of group 7 elements also known   as the halogens.  The most reactive halogen is fluorine and the least reactive is iodine. F 2 >Cl 2 >Br 2 >I 2  Fluorine is the most electronegative (or most reactive) non metal.  However in the presence of light , AgBr is the most reactive, followed by AgCl. ( Br 2 >Cl 2 >I 2 ).  In terms of colour intensity, AgI (yellow) is the most visible, the AgBr  5.   Chlorine gas [Cl 2 gas ]   has two effects on litmus paper.  It turns it from blue to red;   next, it bleaches it.  6.   Cl 2 gas   is greenish yellow while   NO 2 gas   is reddish brown   ( or brown)  7.   Oxygen   rekindles a glowing splint.  N 2 O   rekindles a BRIGHTLY glowing but extinguishes a feeble splint.  It is used as anaesthesia in surgical operation  8.   Cl 2   gas   and   SO 2   gas   are bleaching agents. Both   bleach in the presence of  .   water .   Cl 2   gas   bleaches by oxidation while   SO 2   gas   bleaches by reduction.  Bleached dye by   SO 2   does not last long as that by chlorine. Why?  Because the bleached dye may become reoxidized by atmospheric oxygen to  form the original coloured dye.  This is why a white straw hat often turns yellow after some time .  9.   SO 2   gas   and   H 2 S   gas   are both reducing agents.They will both decolourize   acidified  KMnO 4   (from purple to colourless).  They will also turn   acidified K 2 Cr 2 O 7   from   orange to green.  However, H 2 S gas   gives yellow precipitate with   acidified KMnO 4   and   acidified K 2 Cr 2 O 7  in addition while   SO 2   gas   does not. The yellow precipitate is sulphur.  10.   H 2 S is oxidized to S ulphur   while SO 2   is oxidized to   H 2 SO 4

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   21  NOTE ON GASES 3  1.   Chlorine   and   SO 2   bleach in the presence of water  SO 2   is a reducing agent; it bleaches by reduction.  Cl 2   is an oxidizing agent;it bleaches by oxidation  SO 2   bleaches dye   by reduction while chlorine bleaches it by oxidation .  Bleached dye by   SO 2   does not last long as that by chlorine.  Why?  Be cause the bleached dye may become reoxidized by atmospheric oxygen to  form the original coloured dye.  This is why a white straw hat often turns yellow after some time  2.   Why is hydrogen gas used as oxy - hydrogen flame for melting metals?  Hydrogen gas is highly flammable. It gives out a lot heat when it burns.  Why is hydrogen gas used for filling balloons?   It has low density.  3.   How is hydrogen produced industrially?  I.   By Bosch process   (It uses cok e )  II.   From methane   ( It uses hydocarbons e.g. methane instead of coke)  III.   By   electrolytic methods It   produces very pure hydrogen from brine  ( brine is   concentrated NaCl)  Bosch process involves two stages  i.   The production of water gas   (a mixture of CO and H 2   )which is an endothermic  reaction;  ii.   The reduction of steam to H 2   by CO which is a reversible -   exothermic reaction.  Explanation:  Steam is passed over red - hot coke at about 1200 0 C   to produce water gas.  Next, the excess steam is mixed with the water gas at 450 0 C .  Catalyst:   I ron (III) oxide or chromium (III) oxide.  Finally, the CO in the water gas is converted to CO 2   with a further yield of hydrogen  -   Note that producer gas is a   mixture of CO and N 2 .  However, water gas burns better than producer gas.  -   Producer gas has about 67% non combustible nitrogen.  Generally nitrogen does not support combustion.It is an important diluent.  As a   result, it slows down the rate of combustion and corrosion.  Hydrogen , however, supports combustion

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   22  IMPORTANT NOTE ON AIR  Constituents   of air  Nitrogen gas = 78%  Oxygen = 21%  Carbon(IV) oxide CO 2   = 0.03%  Water vapour = variable  Noble gases = 1%  There are four reasons   air is regarded as a mixture.     It does not have chemical formula.     Its   constituents   cannot be separated by physical means or by using any of the separation  techniques.     Its   constituents   retain their individual properties.     And finally, if each   constituent   of air is mixed in the right proportion, air will be formed  without any evidence of a chemical change.  - Alkalis like NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH) 2   will remove   CO 2   from air.  - D rying agents like conc ontrated . H 2 SO 4   will remove water vapour.  - Alkaline pyrogall ol or heated Copper tunings or p hosphorus will removes O 2  Then, two gases   left   will be   nitrogen and noble gases.     This is why nitrogen prepared in the laboratory weighs   more   than  pure nitrogen.  I ndustrially or commercially,   p ure nitrogen is obtained by   fractional   distillation   of  liquefied air.  Boiling points of nitrogen is − 𝟏𝟗𝟔 ℃   while that of oxygen is − 𝟏𝟖𝟑 ℃ .  During fractional distillation of liquefied   air, nitrogen gas distilled   first because it has lower  melting point than oxyen gas.  QUESTION 1 :  Mention 3   separation techniques which use   method of boiling points .  Evaporation, S imple   distillation   a nd fractional distillation  QUESTION 2:  Which component of distillation plant converts vapour to distillate?  LIEBIG CONDENSER  QUESTION 3:   What is the function of the kipp’s apparatus ?  The   kipp’s apparatus is used to produce or supply any gas whenever it is needed in the  laboratory.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   23  NOTE ON NOBLE GAS  The noble gases are helium, neon, argon etc.     There is one percent noble gas in air.     Of all the noble   gases, argon is the most abundant in the atmosphere.     Argon   is used in gas - filled electric lamps because it helps to prevent the oxidation of the  lamp filament.     Noble gases   give colour lights under reduced pressure and increased voltage.  This is why they used in advertisement signs     Helium is non combustible and almost as light as hydrogen.  This is   why   it is used in observation of balloons unlike hydrogen which is  .   flammable.     Neon lights are use d in aerodrome beacons   -   they have high power of   fog penetration .  FOUNTAIN EXPERIMENT  HCl,   NO 2   and NH 3   are used for fountain experiment because they are extremely  soluble in water. The water becomes acidic and the litmus turns red  AMMONIUM SALTS  Ammonium salts are always decomposed by heat and sometimes sublime.  The best example of sublimate is provided by ammonium chloride.  The characteristic feature of sublimation is that on cooling, the vapour condenses to the solid  without the intermediate   liquid state.  Sublimation is when a substance, on heating, goes   from solid state to a gaseous   state .  The opposite of sublimation is   desublimatio n.  Another substance that sublimes on heat ing   is iodine crystal .  Ammonia gas is always evolved whenever an   ammonium salt decomposes on  heating.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   29  IMPORTANT NOTE ON ANIONS OF ACIDS  1.   HCl   (aq) , H 2 SO 4   (aq) , and HNO 3   (aq)   are strong acids.  Their anions are:   𝑪𝒍 − ( 𝒂𝒒 ) ,   𝑺𝑶 𝟒  𝟐 −  ( 𝒂𝒒 )   and   𝑵𝑶 𝟑  −  ( 𝒂𝒒 )  2.   All anions of strong acids   ( that is   𝑪𝒍 − ( 𝒂𝒒 )   ,   𝑺𝑶 𝟒  𝟐 −  ( 𝒂𝒒 ) ,   𝑵𝑶 𝟑  −  ( 𝒂𝒒 ) )   are   NOT   affected   by  dilute acids.  NOTE  During the test for these anions   𝑪𝒍 − ( 𝒂𝒒 ) ,   𝑺𝑶 𝟒  𝟐 −  ( 𝒂𝒒 )   and   𝑵𝑶 𝟑  −  ( 𝒂𝒒 )     dilute   acids   will always   be   added.     And if any of them is present, there will be no visible change.     This is because   they are not affected by   dilute acids .  3.   H 2 CO 3   (aq)   and H 2 SO 3   (aq)   are weak acids.  Their anions are :   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −  ( 𝒂𝒒 )   and   𝑺𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −  ( 𝒂𝒒 )  4.   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −  ( 𝒂𝒒 )   and   𝑺𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −  ( 𝒂𝒒 ) are anions of weak acids. Once a   dilute   acid is added to either of  them, a gas will be liberated.     𝑺𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −   will   liberate   SO 2 gas   while   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 − will liberate CO 2   gas.  5.   Acids always liberate   H 2 S   from sulphide salts.  2HCl (s)   + FeS (s)   FeCl 2(aq)   + H 2 S (g)  HNO 3(aq)   + PbS (s)   Pb(NO 3 ) 2(aq)   + H 2 S (g)  Whenever an acid is added and nothing happens,  i t is because   𝑯𝑪𝑶 𝟑  −   /   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −   or   𝑯𝑺𝑶 𝟑  −   /   𝑺𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −   or   𝑺 𝟐 −   is absent.  6.   HCO 3   is produced by passing excess CO 2   gas into   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −   or   𝑶𝑯 −   solution.  7.   Sililarly, HSO 3   is produced by passing excess SO 2   gas into   𝑺𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −   or   𝑶𝑯 −   solution.  𝑯𝑪𝑶 𝟑  −   or   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 − will   produce the same reactions since both of them will give off CO 2(gas)  once an acid is added .  So if you write   “   𝑯𝑪𝑶 𝟑  −   or   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 − ” as an inference instead of   𝑪𝑶 𝟑  𝟐 −   ,   you are very right.  𝑯𝑪𝑶 𝟑  −   and   𝑯𝑺𝑶 𝟑  −   are acid salts. Their   solution will always turn litmus red  because of the presence of hydrogen atom in their molecule.  I have removed   𝑯𝑪𝑶 𝟑  −   and   𝑯𝑺𝑶 𝟑  −   in this study because the current WAEC syllabus does  not   include them   among the anions to be studied under qualitative analysis  HOWEVER, w henever   concentrated H 2 SO 4   is added to any salt that has  𝑪𝒍 −   , or   𝑵𝑶 𝟑  −   ,   an   acid will be formed.     𝑵𝑶 𝟑  −   salts will give HNO 3     𝑪𝒍 −   salts will give HCl  Conc. H 2 SO 4   + NaCl   Na 2 SO 4   + HCl  This is one method of preparing strong acids in the laboratory

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   44  IDENTIFYING ORGANIC COMPOUNDS  Unknown salt + Ethanol   If a pleasant fruity smell is   produced, then the  unknown salt is an alkanoic acid while the pleasant fruity smell is   an alkanoate (or Ester).  The process above is known as   ESTERIFICATION ,   while the reverse reaction is  HYDROLYSIS.  Examples of esters inclu de are vegetable oils like palm oil,  groundnut oil , animal fats etc     Esters   have sweet fruity smell.     An ester is slightly soluble in water and is neutral to litmus.  Tollens’ reagent , Benedict’s and Fehling’s reagent can test for aldehyde but will not   identify the individual  compounds.  For specific aldehyde, we use Brady’s reagent.  Brady’s reagent is 2,4 dinitophenylhydrazine dissolved in acidified methanol.  A bright orange or yellow precipitate confirms the presence of (alkanal or aldehyde) or (alkano ne or ketone)  Lucas reagent is a solution of anhydrous zinc chloride(ZnCl2) concentrated hydrochloric acid(HCl)  - Oily layer on heating confirms the presence of primary alkanol  - Oily layer after a while without heating confirms the presence of secondary alk anol  - Oily layer immediately confirms the presence of tertiary alkanol  Sudan III confirms lipid staining

Alkanoic acids or carboxylic acids   are soluble in water and give   CO 2   which turns  lime water { Ca(OH) 2 }milky when they react with   NaHCO 3   or KHCO 3   solution.  Some alkanals and   alkanones also show si milar reactions with the above   reagents,  .   al though   this is not a confirmato ry test for them.     Unsaturated organic compounds give a luminous (sooty or smoking) flame while  the sa turated give non   –   luminous or   non   –   sooty flame.     An example of a saturated hydrocarbon is alkane. Alkenes and alkynes are  unsaturated.     Saturated hydrocarbon can under combustion and substitution reactions while  unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo combustion and addition reactions.     Unsaturate d hydrocarbon decourize bromine water and acidified KMnO 4 .  It changes acidified K 2 Cr 2 O 7   from orange to green.  4.   Terminal alkynes give reddish brown precipitate with ammoniacal copper (l) chloride.  (   CuCl 2 /NH 3 ) or whitish yellow   precipitate   with ammoniacal silver nitrate solution.  This test is used to differentiate alkenes from alkynes.  (   T erminal alkyne has its triple bond   on its first carbon )  5.   Protein gives violet colouration with   Biuret test .  Biuret test is a combination of CuSO 4   + Caustic Soda (NaOH).  6.   Protein also gives white precipitate which turns brick - red on heating with   Millon’s  reagent .  7.   Xanthoproteic reaction(conc. HNO 3   + NH 3 )  It is used to test for proteins  - Add conc.   HNO 3   first to the unknown solution.  - A white precipitate will be formed which turns yellow on heating.  - Cool the contents and add few drops of ammonia solutions (a base).  - The precipitate deepens to orange.  8.   Ninhydrin test  When proteins are boiled   with   a dilute aqueous   solution of Ninhydrin,  .   a   purple colour   is produced.  - Protein is not soluble in water but it is hydrolysed to give amino acid when boiled  .   with solution of   HCl   or   NaOH .  Using   paper chromatography, the amino acid can be identified.

Solubility curve   is a graphical representation which shows the extent of solubility of  salts   in a given solvent at different temperature.     The solubility of   solid   solutes increases as temperature increases.     Apart from HCl gas, the solubility of   gases   increases as pressure increases but decreases  with increase in temperature.  APPLICATION OF SOLUBILITY (SOLUBILITY CURVE)  (1)   To determine the amount of solutes that can be dissolved in a given volume of a  particular solvent.  (2)   To determine t he most suitable solvent for a particular solutes  (3)   To know the bes t method to apply in separation   of a given mixture of solutes  SOLUBLE IN WATER   INSOLUBLE IN WATER  1. ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   50  ACID   – BASE   INDICATORS /BUFFER SOLUTIONS  BUFFER SOLUTION  A buffer solution is one which resists changes in   pH   on dilution or addition of small amount of  acid   or alkalis.  In other words, it   keeps its   pH   approximately constant when small amounts of an acid or alkali  are added.  It   is widely used in processed foods   and drinks to prevent excess acidity.  EXAMPLES  They usually consist of a weak acid or weak base in the presence of one of its salts.  -   Aqueous ammonia and NH 4 Cl  -   H 2 CO 3   and NaHCO 3  -   CH 3 COOH and CH 3 COONa  Acid buffers keep the   pH   below 7  They consist of weak acid plus salt of weak acid  e.g.   CH 3 COOH and CH 3 COONa  Alkaline buffers keep the   pH   above 7  They consist of weak alkali plus salt of weak alkali  NH 3(aq)   and NH 4 Cl  ACID   – BASE   INDICATORS  Indicators are weak organic acids or bases which will produce different colours  in   solutions according to the hydrogen ion (H + ) concentration in that solution     Methyl orange is used for strong acid against weak base (or   𝐶𝑂 3  2 − salts)     Phenolphthalein is used for strong base against weak acids.     Methyl red is used for strong acids against strong base, although any  indicator could be used.  INDICATOR   ACID   NEUTRAL  or end point  BASE  Litmus   Red   Purple   Blue  Methyl orange   red   Orange   Yellow  Methyl red   Red   Red   Yellow  Phenolphthalein   Colourless   Colourless   Pink

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   51  CONJUGATE ACID   AND BASE  Hydrogen ion ( H + )   is also called a proton  Acids are proton (or H + ) donors  Bases are proton (or H + )   acceptors donors.  According to Bronsted - Lowry, a conjugate acid constitutes of two substances that differ by the  presence of a proton.  When an acid donates a proton, it changes into a base and when a base accepts a proton, it  becomes an acid.  In other w ords ,  A p roton acceptor   is   called   a   base   and   the product   formed is called   a   conjugate acid .  Conjugate acid   =   base plus hydrogen ion (H + )   [or proton]  BASE + H +   = CONJUGATE ACID  B+ H =   BH  This means that B= BASE   and   BH= CONJUGATE ACID  A proton donor   is   called   an   acid   and   the product   formed is called   a   conjugate base .  Conjugate base = acid minus hydrogen ion (H + )   [or proton]  ACID   -   H +   = CONJUGATE BASE  AH - H   =   A  This means that AH   = ACID   and   A= CONJUGATE BASE  Example 1  NH 3   + H +   ⇋   NH 4 +  From reactant to product  H +   is   gained  Therefore, NH 3   = base  It is the Proton acceptor  NH 4 +   = conjugate acid  Why?   It is the product  Therefore,  NH 4 +   is the conjugate acid of NH 3  LET ME EXPLAIN IT FURTHER  From the reactant side,  NH 3   + H +  - This means NH 3   has accepted a proton  - And proton acceptors are called base.  - Therefore NH 3   is a base  - NH 4 +   is the product formed  It is the conjugate acid of NH 3  NH 3   + H +   ⇋   NH 4 +  base   conjugate acid  Example 2  NH 4 +   ⇋   NH 3   +   H +  From reactant to product  H +   is lost  Therefore,   NH 4 +   = acid  It is the Proton donor   ( or giver or loser )  NH 3 = conjugate base  Why?   It is the product  Therefore,  NH 3   is called the conjugate base of  NH 4 +  NOTE  The weaker the acid, the stronger the  conjugate base the stronger the acid, the  weaker the conjugate base.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   53  AMPHIPROTIC /AMPHOTERIC   SUBSTANCES  A mphiprotic molecules or ions are substances which can either donate or accept a proton (or H + )  1.   They have hydrogen to donate  2.   They can accept proton from other compounds.  Examples:   water, ammonia, HCO 3 -   and HSO 3 -  A mphoteric substance s will act as   acid s   when they react   with base s   and   they will act as   base s when  they   react with acid s .  Note  Amphoteric substances do not have hydrogen to donate .  Example 1  1.   H 2 O (l)   ⇋   OH -   (aq)   +   H + (aq)  Acid   conjugate base  H 2 O (l)   donates proton = it is an acid  Therefore, the product is the conjugate  base  1.   H 2 O   (l)   +   H +   (aq)   ⇋   H 3 O + (aq)  base   conjuga te acid  H 2 O (l)   accepts proton = it is a base  Therefore, the product is the conjugate acid  Water served as the base in the acid and as the acid in the base in the examples above  F -   +   H +   ⇋   HF  HF   ⇋   F -   +   H +  QUESTIONS:  What is the conjugate acid or the conjugate base of   each of the   following?  1.   HCl   2.   CH 3 NH 2   3 .   OH -   4 .   HCO 3 -  ANSWERS  1.   HCl   ⇋   H +   Cl -  Acid   conjugate base  2.   CH 3 NH 2   +   H +   ⇋   CH 3 NH 3 +  Base   conjugate acid  3.   OH -   +   H +   ⇋   H 2 O  Base   conjugate acid  HCO 3 -   is amphiprotic.  It can donate proton and it can accept proton.  In other words, it has H +   to give and it can accept   additional H +  4.   HCO 3 -   +   H +   ⇋   H 2 CO 3  Base   conjugate acid  OR  HCO 3 -   ⇋   CO 3 2 -   +   H +  Acid   conjugate base

The   𝑶𝑯 − of other metals   decompose on heating to give   water ( H 2 O )   and metallic oxides e.g.  Ca(OH) 2   CaO +H 2 O     The oxides of K +   to Al 3+   do not decompose on heating .     They are   not   reduced by reducing agents   like   hydrogen, coke or CO   etc.  This is why metals from potassium to aluminium are extracted by electrolysis.     The   oxides of Zn 2+   to Cu 2+   do not decompose on heating but   they   are reduced by  hydrogen, coke or CO  This is why they are extracted by reduction of their oxides  The formation the protective layer of PbO interferes with the reaction   of lead  with water under normal conditions.  Metals   Extraction  K and Na   Electrolysis of fused hydroxides and chlorides  Ca and Mg   Electrolysis of fused chlorides  Al   Electrolysis of oxides  Zn to Cu   First, r oast   their carbonates or sulphides to form   oxides.  Next , r eduction their oxides by H 2 , CO or carbon  Hg and Ag   Roasting in air  Au   Mined as free element  Where copper of high quality is required, electrolytic reduction is applied  where the crude or impure copper is made the anode

This is why   Fe and Al   containers are used in transporting conc.   HNO 3     Washing soda   ( Na 2 CO 3 .10H 2 O ) is never used to clean aluminum vessel because  .   aluminum is soluble in both sodium and potassium hydroxides.     Ca(OH) 2   in solid form is called slake lime  Ca(OH) 2   in solution form is called lime water     Sodium is always stored under paraffin oil, or toluene or   naphtha.  Why?     To prevent   its oxidation by the atmospheric gases  (e.g. oxygen & CO 2 )  Na (s)   + O 2(g)   Na 2 O  Na 2 O + H 2 O   NaOH + H 2  NaOH + CO 2(g)   Na 2 CO 3     Corrosion   always   occurs in the presence of oxygen   (or air)   and water.  It increases if   CO 2   or SO 2   is present.     The corrosion of iron is called rusting  The   brownish   substance formed after the corrosion of iron is called rust.  Rust is Fe 3+       Rusting of iron is an example of corrosion.     It is an electrochemical process. It is   not   an electrolytic process.     However, the electroplating of iron is electr olytic (or electrolysis )  Rusting takes   place in the presence of air (oxygen) and water.  Rusting occurs at the anodic region (oxidation)  Fe   (s)   Fe 2+ (aq)   + 2e -  Fe 2+ (aq)   + 2OH -   Fe(OH) 2   (s)  Fe(OH) 2   (s)   + dissolved oxygen   Rust   (FeO 3 .   𝑥 H 2 O)  Rusting of iron is prevented by a layer of zinc or other reactive metal which acts as  a sacrificial anode.

They make OXIDATION possible. This is why, they are called oxidizing agents .  TEST FOR OXIDIZING AGENTS  (1). They oxidize green iron (II) Chloride(FeCl 2 ) to brown Fe 3+  (Fe 2+   Fe 3+ )  Oxidation always produces   an   increase in oxidation number   (+ 2 to +3 )  (2). They oxidize hydrogen sulphide gas (H 2 S) to yellow deposit of sulphur  (S 2 -   S 0 )  Oxidation always produces   an   increase in oxidation number ( -   2 to 0 )  TEST FOR REDUCING AGENT  METALS are called electron donors or electropositive elements.  They make REDUCTION possible. Therefore,   they are called reducing agents.  (1)   They turn the purple colour of acidified KMnO 4   to colourless  ( That is, they decolourize acidified KMnO 4   )  MnO -   (purple)   Mn 2+  Purple   colourless  Reduction   always produces   a decrease   in oxidation number   ( from +7 to +2)  (2)   They turn acidified K 2 Cr 2 O 7   from orange to green.  Cr 2 O 7 2 -   (orange)   2Cr 3+   (green)  Reduction   always produces   a   decrease   in oxidation number   ( from +6 to +3)  RECALL:  SO 2   and H 2 S are both reducing agents.Both of them will decolourize acidified KMnO 4   and  turn acidified K 2 Cr 2 O 7   from orange to green.  H 2 S gives yellow   precipitate (of sulphur) in addition but SO 2   does not  QUESTION:  When H ₂ S gas is passed into a solution of iron (III) chloride, the colour changes  from yellow to green. This is because  A. H ₂ S is reduced to S   B.   ions are oxidized by H ₂ S  C. ions are oxidized by ions   D. ions are reduced to Fe 2+   ions.  The correct answer is D

H 2 SO 4  Efflorescence   is a pheno menon whereby some crystalline   substances lose all or some part of  their water of crystallization when exposed to the atmosphere.  e.g.  Na 2 CO 3 .10H 2 O   - 9H2O   Na 2 CO 3 .H 2 O  Washing soda  Efflorescent is the salt   that exhibits efflorescence.  Anhydrous Na 2 SO 4   is called salt cake, while Na 2 SO 4 . 10H 2 O is called Glauber’s   salt.  Anhydrous Na 2 CO 3   is called   Soda ash   while   Na 2 CO 3.   10H 2 O   is   called   washing soda  Deliquescent   substances absorb water when exposed to the atmosphere  and turn to solution.   In other words, they absorb water and dissolve in it to form soltions  Hydroscopic   substances absorb water but do not t urn to solution. If they are solids, they  become sticky or moist but if liquid ,   they become diluted   .e.g.   concentrated H 2 SO 4  DRYING AGENTS  These are substances that have strong affinity for moisture or water. They may be deliquescent  or   hydroscopic substances.  They are used in drying gases. They are also used in   dessicators   for drying salts.  A drying agent cannot be used if it reacts with the substance to be dried.  QUESTION:   Why is Conc. H 2 SO 4   not used in drying ammonia?  ANSWER   :   Ammonia reacts with concentrated H 2 SO 4  2NH 3(g)   + H 2 SO 4(aq)   (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4(aq)  DRYING AGENT   GASES  Conc.H 2 SO 4   All   gases except ammonia   and hydrogen sulphide  Fuse CaCl 2   All gases except ammonia  Calcium oxide   ( CaO or quicklime )   Suitable for ammonia in particular  Anhydrous CaCl 2   is used in a dessicator for drying salts and as drying   agents for all gases except  ammonia gas ( NH 3   (g)   ) .  Although Silica gel can be used to dry all gases but it is not in the WAEC syllabus.  COLLECTION OF GASES

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   65  COLLECTION OF GASES  Lighter than air   Heavier than air  examples   H 2 , NH 3   examples   CO 2 , HCl,SO 2  Collected by the   downwards displacement   of  air   or you say by   upwards delivery  Collected by the   upwards displacement of air  or you say, by   downwards delivery  EXPLANATION  Hydrogen is lighter than air .THEREFORE ,   during   its   collection through a delivery  tube, hydrogen will be   up   while the air will be   down  So hydrogen is collected by   up wards   delivery or we say by   down wards  displacement of air.  However, chlorin e gas   is heavier than air .THEREFORE, during its collection through a  delivery tube, chlorine gas will be down while th e air will be up.  So chlorine   gas is collected by downwards delivery or we say by upwards  displacement of air.  Nitrogen and Oxygen are not collected by the displacement of air  WHY?  Because they have roughly the same density as air.  Nitrogen prepared   from air is denser than pure nitrogen.  Why?  It contains one percent noble gas.  1. A gas that can be collected over water in the laboratory is?  A.   Hydrogen chloride   B.   Ammonia   C.   Sulphur (IV) oxide   D.   Oxygen  ANSWER= D   (oxygen cannot be collected by the displacement of air)  2.   The best way of collecting chlorine is  A.   by downward s   displacement of air   B. by upward s   displacement of air  C.   over water   D. under water  ANSWER= B

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   68  OXIDES  Oxides are formed when elements combine with   oxygen .  element + oxygen = oxide  There are different types oxides depending on the type of element o r the amount of  oxygen involved in the formation of the oxide.  (1)   BASIC OXIDES  These are oxides of metals.  They form base when they react with water e.g ,Na 2 O,   K 2 O, CaO etc  (2)   ACIDIC OXIDES  These are oxides of non - metals.  They react with water to form acids e.g. CO 2   SO 2   SO 3   NO 2   etc.  They are also known as   acid anhydrides.  An acid anhydrides are non - metallic oxides which dissolve in  water to produce acids.  (3)   AMPHOTERIC OXIDES  They have both acidic and basic properties  When they react with acid, they form salt and water only.  ZnO (s)   + H 2 SO 4(aq)   ZnSO 4(aq)   + H 2 O (l)  But with alkalis or base, they form complex salts  ZnO,Al 3 O 2 , PbO, SnO etc.  ( Their metallic ions (or   cations   )   are soluble in excess of NaOH)  Al 2 O 3(s)   +2NaOH (aq)   +3H 2 O (l)   2NaAl(OH) 4(aq)  (4)   NEUTRAL OXIDES:  They are neither acidic nor basic e.g. N 2 O , CO, H 2 O etc.  PEROXIDES  Peroxides contains higher amount of oxygen than the ordinary oxides. Na 2 O 2,   CaO 2   BaO 2.  General oxides have oxidation number of   - 2 but peroxides have   - 1.  They yield hydrogen peroxides   on reaction with dilute acids.  BaO 2   + H 2 SO 4   BaSO 4   + H 2 O 2  They are used as bleaching agents     They are   unstable compound.They easily release oxygen when they are heated.     This is why oxygen is prepared by the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.  2H 2 O 2(l)   MnO2   2H 2 O (g)   + O 2(g)   (H eating   is not necessary   )  Other methods of preparing oxygen include:     2   KClO 3   MnO2   KCl + O 2   (with heating is necessary )     5H 2 O 2(l)   + 2KMnO 4(aq)   + 3H 2 O (aq)   K 2 SO 4(aq)   + 2MnSO 4(a q)   + 8H 2 O (l)   + 5O 2(g)

The light or radiations act as catalyst.  This reaction is common   with   the halogens.  1.   Reaction of methane with chlorine  2.   Reaction of chlorine with water etc.  The   reactions   above   require light to proceed  The reaction of chlorine   is known as photochemical reaction because they are  influenced by light.  Other examples   include     The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide     Photosynthesis in plants     Conversion of silver halides to grey metallic silver  (used in photography).  DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THERMAL AND DOUBLE DECOMPOSITION     Thermal dissociation is a reversible reaction brought about by the application of heat  NH 4 Cl   (aq)   ⇋   NH 3(g)   + HCl (g)  N 2 O 4(g)   ⇋   2NO 2 (g)     D ouble decomposition   is a type of decomposition in which the salt decomposes to form   two  new substances by exchange of radicals  CuSO 4   + H 2 S   →   CuS   +   H 2 SO 4  NaCl + H 2 SO 4   →   NaHSO 4   + HCl  Hints: double decomposition   involves exchange of wives  Cu SO 4   +   H 2   S   →   CuS   +   H 2 SO 4  SO 4   will go to   H   S   will go to   Cu  This is one method of producing insoluble salts apart from direct   combination.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   70  WATER TREATMENT PLANT  Polyelectrolyte s are chemical flocculants used in water treatment to   facilitate  floc c ulation or coagulation.   An example is potash alum or   simply alum.  After coagulation , the water is allowed to sediment; then after it goes through filteration before  other chemical substances are added to kill germs and improve on the quality of the water.  Chlorine is added to kill germs.  Flourine is added   to prevent tooth decay and iodine is added to prevent goitre  After sedimentation is aeration     It exposes the water to a large amount of air and the resulting oxidation kills micro   –  organism.Chlorine, which is a sterilizing agent is added to kill the   remaining germs.     Excess of chlorine   makes the water to have colour , taste and odour.  Ca(OH)2 is, therefore, added to correct the PH and to improve the taste of water     The PH of water for towns hip supply is always between   7 and   8.5 .  If the PH of water is less than 7, the water will be acidic and will corrode the pipes.  Pipe - borne water from the water works is usually hard.  And If the water has to be used in industry, it has to be softened.  HARDNESS OF WATER  Hard water does not produce lather with soap and it often leads to wastage of soap.  There are two types of hardness of water.  1.   Temporary hardness   2. Permanent hardness     Tempo rary hardness of water is caused by   Ca(HCO 3 ) 2   and Mg(HCO 3 ) 2  And they can be removed by: boiling or adding   Ca(OH) 2 . They form scales inside  kettles and pots.   This is known as furring.  Permanent hardness of water is caused by   Ca 2+   and Mg 2+   in the  form of   SO 4 2 -   and   𝑪𝒍 −   (CaSO 4 , MgSO 4 ,CaCI 2   and   MgCI 2 ).     They are removed by using chemicals like:  Na 2 CO 3 ,NaOH   (caustic soda) and permutit or zeolite     Permutit or zeolite is an ion   – exchange   resin used industrially and in   homes for  softening water   .  NOTE:   Na 2 CO 3   removes both permanent and temporary hardness.  Reasons     Boiling is used in removing temporary harness in water  because   𝑯𝑪 𝑶 𝟑  −   is always decomposed on heating.     However, permanent hardness is caused by   SO 4 2 -  and   𝑪𝒍 − of metals which cannot be decomposed by heat  Hardness of water forms   stalactites and stalagmites   in rocks and caves. stalac T ites  grows at the   TOP   (or upwards ) while stala G mites grows at the   GROUND   (or downwards)

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   71  COLLOIDAL SOLUTION  Hints: SLG.SL   L3G2   SELF.SF  Dispersed solute  or substance  Dispersion medium  or solvent   Example   EXPLANATION  S =S O LID   L =LIQUID   S =Sols   solid   dispersed in liquid  L =LIQUID   L =LIQUID   E =Emulsions   liquid dispersed in liquid  G= GAS   L =LIQUID   LF =Lather &foam   Gas dispersed in liquid  S =SOLID   G= GAS   S =Smoke   Solid dispersed in gas  L =LIQUID   G= GAS   F =Fog   Liquid dispersed in gas  SLG.SL   L3G2   SELF.SF   solid   dispersed in liquid  Smoke can also be liquid dispersed in gas  - Emulsions   are milk,hair cream,butter  - Fog   includes sprays,aerosols,insecticides,deodorants  - Sols   are starch,glue,   jelly   ,   solid sols is gel  - Soap and   detergent are emulsing agent s . Both can form emulsion     True solution   can pass or diffuse through semi permeable membrane   (DIALYSIS)  while   colloidal or false solution   can scatter light   (Tyndall effects).     Unlike   suspension , particles of true and false   solutions are too small to been with the  eyes.     While a true solution is a uiform or homogeneous mixture, suspension is a  heterogeneous mixture. Therefore, a solid - liquid suspension can be separated using  filtration.  NOTE ON   SOLUTIONS  - A solution which can dissolve more solute at a given temperature is described as an  unsaturated solution .It is described as an “unsatisfied solution”  - A saturated solution   dissolves   all the solute it can dissolve   at a given temperature in the  presence of undissolved solute. You can call it a “satisfied solution”.  - A supersatur ated   solution   dissolves more solute than it should have at a particular  solution. You can call it a “greedy solution”  It is an unstable sol ution because any roughing handling can cause t he crystallization of the salt  HINTS:  Nobles gases and alkanes behave like saturated solution. Noble gases have completely filled outermost  shells. The alkanes are described as saturated hydrocarbons.  The   noble gases and the alkanes are filled or satisfied.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   74  EXTRACTIONS OF METALS     Most metals are found in combined forms of more or less definite chemical   composition  known as minerals.     Minerals plus earthy materials gives ores  Ores are usually concentrated and changed to oxides before extrations.  Why?  It is easier to deal with oxides than sulphide and trioxocarbonates (IV).  Thus if the ore   is not an oxide , the ore concentrate is usually roasted in air to change it to an  oxide.  Ores are   usually   concentrated in 3 ways  1.   By washing: this leaves behind the heavier ores. E.g. tin ores  2.   By magnetic separator e.g. copper ore s  3.   By froth - flotation. E.g. Zn ores  Froth is the churning up of ore with oil and water which is the skimmed off by  blowing air  1.  Extraction of sodium:   Electrolysis of fuse NaCl  Name of electrolytic cell:   Downs cell  Anode :   graphite rods  Cathode:   steel cylinder  Electrolyte:   fuse NaCl  Note     To make the reaction economically feasible, CaCl 2   is usually added to the lower the  melting point of NaCl from   800℃   𝑡𝑜   600℃ .     Sodium can easily be cut ; very malleable and soft

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   75  1.   Extraction of calcium:   Electrolysis of fuse CaCl 2  Name of electrolytic cell: Downs cell  Anode :   graphite  Cathode: iron rod  Electrolyte: fuse CaCl 2  It produces   calcium and chlorine.  Note     To make the reaction economically feasible, CaF 2   is usually added to the lower the  melting point of CaCl 2   from   850℃   𝑡𝑜   650℃ .     CaCl 2   is   a by -   product of the solvay process  3.   Extraction of aluminium  Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust.  Name of electrolytic cell:   Hall process  Anode :   graphite lining  Cathode:   graphite rods  Electrolyte:   Pure molten   alumina (Al 2 O 3 )   in cryolite (Na 3 AlF 6 )  Temperature   :   950   ℃     Main source of aluminium is bauxite (Al 2 O 3 .2H 2 O)     The bauxite ore is first purified using aqueous NaOH before mixing it with  molten cryolite which serves as solvent for the ore.  The process very expensive for some reasons  1.   High temperature makes the process very expensive  2.   Oxygen is given out at the anode.  As a result, the anode is continuous burnt off and has to be replaced.  How pure alumina is produced  The bauxite is first heated with caus tic soda solution (concentrated NaOH) to give sodium  aluminate (III)   [ NaAl(OH) 4 ]  The impurities are iron (III) oxide and trioxosilicate (IV) do not dissolve in caustic soda. Thus  they are filtered off.  The filterate which is sodium aluminate (III)( NaA l(OH) 4 )   is seeded with aluminium hydroxide  crystal to induce the precipitation of more aluminium hydroxide.  The aluminium hydroxide precipitate is then filtered, washed , dried and then heated strongly  to yield pure aluminium oxide or alumina Al 2 O 3

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   76  4.  Extraction of iron.   (The blast furnance)  Ores of iron include : Haematite   Fe 2 O 3   and   Magnetite Fe 3 O 4  The iron ores are first roasted in air so that iron (III) oxide is produced.  Raw materials for solvay process  1.   Iron (III) oxide   ( Fe 2 O 3 )  2.   Coke   (C)  3.   Lime stone   (   CaCO 3   )  The ingredients are loaded from the top while a blast of hot air is introduced from the bottom  through small pipes ( tuyeres)  The   blast furnance maintains 2 temperatures.  1.   The lower   region of the furnance at   temperature   of   2000℃ : This the region where the  white - hot coke is oxidized by oxygen from the hot air to liberate CO 2  C (s)   + O 2(g)   CO 2(g)  2.   The upper   region of the furnance at a   temperature   of   200   ℃   : at this region, the air  lessens and the CO 2   produced earlier is reduced to CO by the white hot coke.  C   (s)   +   CO 2(g)   CO (g)  Finally the CO then reduce the iro n (III) oxide to iron.  Fe 2 O 3(s)   + CO (g)   Fe (l)   CO 2(g)  The limestone decomposes  CaCO 3(s)   CaO (s)   +   CO 2(g)  The   CaO   removes the impurities silicon (IV) oxide as calcium trioxosilicate (IV)  SiO 2(s)   +   CaO (s)   CaSiO 3(s)  The type of iron obtained in the blast furnance is called PIG IRON.  Further improvement on the pig iron gives CAST IRON.  Cast iron is brittle and cannot be be forged.

An alloy is a substance prepared by adding one or more   elements to a base or parent metal to  obtain desirable properties. The added elements are usually metals or carbon. At the cathode, chlorine gas is produced while at the anode, sodium amalgam is produced. Heat of solution   is the energy change when one mole of a substance is dissolved  Heat of formation   is the energy change when one mole of a substance is formed from its  element s .  Heat of   c ombust ion   is the energy change when one mole of a substance is burnt  Heat of   v aporization   is the energy change when one mole of a substance is melted  HEAT CONTENT (H), ENTROPY (S), AND FREE ENERY(G)     Entropy   is a measure of the degree of disorder or rand omness of a substance.  In other, where there is no disorder at all, entropy will be zero.  This means, gases have higher entropy compared to solids and liquids.     Free energy   is the energy available for doing work.     In othe r words, it is the force which brings about a chemical change. ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   85  RATES OF CHEMICAL REACTIONS  AND EQULIBRIUM CONSTANT (Kc )  COLLISION THEORY  For a chemical reaction to occur, the colliding reactants must possess a certain minimum  amount of energy called   activation energy.  To increase the rate of a reaction is to reduce the time taken for product to be formed.  There are factors that can increas e the rate of chemical reactions.  1.   Nature of reactants   :   This include s   solid in lumps or powered form or   salt in   solid ,  liquid or gas.  2.   Temperature :  increases the energy content of the reactants and increases the frequency of collision  changes   equilibrium constant  3.   Concentration   – for solid and liquid : it only increases the frequency of collision.  It does not change equilibrium constant (K C )  4.   Pressure   - for gases:it only increases the frequency of collision  It does not change equilibrium constant   (K C )  5.   Surface area: it only increases the frequency of collision  It does not change equilibrium constant (K C )     The concentration of solids and liquids reactants is unaffected by changes in pressure.     If temperature , concentration or   pressure and surface are a are increased, generally, the  rate of a chemical reaction will increase.     A powder solid has a larger surface area than a large lump of the same solid.  6.   Catalyst :e.g. Light or sunshine is an example.  It   lowers the activation energy. It does not change   equilibrium constant  (K C ).However, it makes equilibrium to be reached more quickly   .  Catalysis is a reaction driven by catalyst  By the way, what are catalysts?

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   86  A   CATALY ST  A   Catalyst   is   substance that alter s the rate   of   a   reaction which remain s   unchanged in  chemical nature and in   mass at the end of the reaction .     It   is   specific in   its   action.   However,   it   cannot start   a   reaction .     And because   it   do es   NOT affect the overall reaction,   it is   always   written above the  arrow   of a   chemical   equation.     It   provide s   different pathway for   a   reaction   which ha s   lower activation energy  than the original route.  A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium;     It increases the rate of the backward reaction to the same extent as the  forward reaction.  In other words, by providing a   lower activation energy, it is easier for the  reactants to surmount the ene rgy barriers and at the   same   time, it is also easier  for the products to revert to reactants.     For this reason, a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium  but it will mean that equilibrium is achieved more rapidly.     E nzymes are natural catalyst a nd   proteins.  LET’S DEFINE EQUILIBRIUM CONSTANT  Equilibrium constant  Equilibrium constant   is the ratio of the speed of the product to the speed of the  reactants. It is always constant. However, only change in temperature can   alter it.  The reaction rate is directly proportional to the concentration of the reactants.  For gaseous systems, pressure is directly proportional to concentration.  At equilibrium,   the reactants are changed into products at the same rate as the  products   are reacting back to give reactants.  Change in concentration,   or   pressure,   or   the use of a catalyst ha s   NO effect on  equilibrium constant but   each of them   will often change the rate at which  equilibrium is achieved.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   88  LE CHATELIER’S PRINCIPLE  Le Chatelier’s Principle states that if a constraint is placed on an equilibrium mixture, then the  equilibrium will shift so as to oppose the constraint.  For ex ample if the temperature is increased, then the equilibrium will shift so as to reduce the  temperature.  According to Le Chatelier’s principle, if an external constraint such as change in temperature,  pressure, or concentration is imposed on a chemical system   in equilibrium   , the equilibrium  will shift so as to annul or neutralize the constraint.  In other wo rds, if a chemical system is in equilibrium and   one of the factors involved in  the equilibrium is altered , the equilibrium will shift so as to annul the effect of the change.  Th e factors or external constraints could be temperature, pressure, concentratio n etc.  21.   Equilibrium constant is the ratio of the speed of product to the speed of  reactants.  𝑲𝒄   =   [ 𝒔𝒑𝒆𝒆𝒅   𝒐𝒇   𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒅𝒖𝒄𝒕 ]  [ 𝒔𝒑𝒆𝒆𝒅   𝒐𝒇   𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒄𝒕𝒂𝒏𝒕𝒔 ]  22.   Change in temperature changes the equilibrium   constant.  23.   Other factors like concentration, pressure, catalyst do not change the value  of equilibrium constant.  EXPLANATION A:   For an endothermic reaction :  - An increase in temperature favours the production of more of the product.  -   Once a forward re action is favoured and more product is produced ,  the equilibrium constant will increase.  In other words, endothermic reactions need HEAT and if heat is supplied, the forward  reaction will be favoured.  Thus, equilibrium constant will increase.  EXPLANAT ION B:   For an exothermic reaction:  - An increase in temperature favours the backward reaction .This means , more of the reactants  will be formed.  -   Once a backward reaction is favoured , more reactants are produced and the equilibrium  constant will decrea se.  In other words, for a forward reaction, exothermic reactions do not need HEAT but if heat is  supplied, the reaction reverses.  This means, a backward reaction will be favoured according to Le chatelier’s Principle.  Thus, equilibrium constant will decre ase.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   89  EFFECT OF PRESSURE  Pressure affects gases only .  L et us consider the following gaseous  equations  Example 1  N 2 O 4(g)   ⇋   2NO 2 (g)  1   2  Low   high  The reaction goes from 1 mole to 2 moles  That is, from low to high  Interpretation  Pressure   is used with gases only .  From the arrows ,  lower pressure will favour the forward  reaction and more NO 2 (g)   will be produced;  while higher pressure will favour the  reversed reaction and more N 2 O 4(g)   will be  produced  EXAMPLE 2  2SO 3(g)   ⇋   3SO 2(g)  2=low   3=high  The reaction goes from 2 moles to 3 moles.  Interpretation  From the arrow s,  lower pressure will favour the forward  reaction and more SO 2(g)   will be produced;  while higher pressure will favour reverse  reaction and more SO 3(g)   will be produced  EXAMPLE 3  H 2(g)   +   I 2(g)   ⇋   2HI (g)  1+1 =2   2  Both sides have the same pressure.  The reaction goes from 2 moles to 2 moles.  Interpretation  Pressure has no effect  Equilibrium will not   shift.  EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE ON:  (A)  EXOTHERMIC REACTIONS  A +B   ⇋   AB   –   HEAT  In exothermic reactions heat is given out  MINUS HEAT   means LOWER  TEMPERATURE will favour the forward  reaction.  Equilibrium shift to right as the equilibrium  constant increases.  However, if the temperature is increased, the  reversed reaction is favoured.  The equilibrium constant reduces as the  equilibrium shift to the left which is the  reactant side.  (B).  ENDOTHERMIC REACTIONS  A+B   ⇋   AB + HEAT  In   endothermic reactions heat is absorded  from the surroundings  PLUS HEAT   means HIGHER  TEMPERATURE will favour the forward  reaction.  Thus, the equilibrium will shift to the right  which is the product side.  This will also increase the equilibrium  constant.  However, if the temperature is reduced, the  reversed reaction is favoured.  The equilibrium constant reduces as the  equilibrium shift to the left which is the  reactant side.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   142  INTRODUCTION TO QUANTITATIVE  (VOLUMETRIC) ANALYSIS  AIM:   To estimate the quantities of certain substance (often acid or   alkalis)   in solution  using a standard solution  STANDARD SOLUTION  This is a solution, which contain a known mass of solute in a given volume of solution.  It is a solution with a known concentrate either in gram per dm 3   (gdm - 3 ) or in mole per  dm 3   (moldm - 3 ).  Once you know the mole or mass of the solute in a given volume of a solvent, then you  have been given a standard solution  GRASP THIS!  SOLUTE + SOLVENT   SOLUTION  Put   10g of NaCl in a flask of capacity 1dm 3   (1000cm) and fill it with water to the highest  mark. Close and shake the mixture very wel l. Good! The solution is now a standard  s olution   .  MOLAR SOLUTION  This is the second kind of solution one need s   to be familiar with in quantitative analysis.  It is c omparable to standard solution in all respec t expect that it relates to one   which  contain one mole (molar mass) of the compound in one dm 3   of the solution.  Catch this!  1 mole of KOH = its molar mass  = 39 + 16 + 1  = 56g  If this 56g of KOH is made of dissolve in a flask of capacity 1 dm 3   ( or   100cm 3 )   of water ,  the n the   resulting solution becomes a molar solution of KOH.  CONCENTRATION  Every solution (whether standard or molar) must have concentration.  Concentration of a solution can be defined as a measure of the amount of  solute contained in a given volume of the solution.  It can be in moldm - 3   or gdm - 3     Concentration can be likened to   TASTE.  For instance, if one put 10g of sugar (solute) in a cup   A   with 20cm 3   of water (solvent),  and 50g of sugar (solvent) in another cup   B,   with 20cm 3   of water (solvent),  which of the two solutions do you think will be sweeter?  …yes?

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   143  Cup B!  Very correct.  Instead of sugar, if one uses NaCl salt, cup   B   will be   saltier, isn’t it?  Yes Sir!  Very good!  Therefore, the sweetness or the saltiness or the bitterness or the taste of a solution is known as  its   what?  Concentration!  Now go over the definition once again.  TYPES OF CONCENTRATION  Concentration can be expressed in two ways:  Mass concentration  Molar concentration  (1)   Mass Concentration  This is used when concentration is expressed in grammes per dm 3   (g/dm 3   or gd - 3 ).  It refers to the mass of solute that will always be found in every one dm 3   of a given solvent.  ( where 1dm 3   = 1000cm 3 )  (2)   Molar concentration  This is the concentration in moles per dm 3   (mol/dm 3   or moldm - 3 ).  It is also called molarity. It is sometimes represented with the symbol, M, e.g. 0.1M means  0.1moldm - 3.  It is the amount in moles of a solute present in one dm 3   a particular   solution.  Go over Molar Solutio n once again  NOTE:  Molar solution is   one mole   in one dm 3   while molar concentration can be in   any mole   in  one dm 3 .  In other words, all molar solutions are standard solutions but all standard solutions are not  molar solutions  LET’S DIG ON  To have better understanding of this aspect of chemistry practical, it is important to have sound  knowledge of   MOLE CONCEPT   and general knowledge of acids, bases and salts

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   144  ACIDS  An acid is a substance which produces hydrogen ions H +   (or protons) as the only positive ions  when dissolved in water.  An acid can also be defined as a substance   which in aqueous solution produces oxonium ions,  H 3 O +   as the only positive ions.  HCl, HNO 3   and H 2 SO 4   are regarded as strong acid because they ionize completely in water  giving H +   and anions.  E.g.  HCl   H +   +   Cl -  HNO 3   H +   +   NO 3 -   ANIONS  H 2 SO 4   2H +   +   SO 4 2 -  The other acids are regarded as weak acids since they only ionize partially in water.  Their solutio ns have low concentration of hydrogen ions e.g. ethanoic acid, H 2 CO 3   , H 3 PO 4 ,  H 2 SO 3   etc.  BASICITY OF AN ACID  This is defined as the number of replaceable hydrogen ions (H + ) in one molecule   of an acid.  The basicity of   H Cl,   H NO 3 , CH 3 COO H   (ethanoic acid) is one.  Why?  Only one hydrogen ion can be replaced in one molecule of their solutions.  Hence, they are said to be monobasic  H 2 SO 4 ,   H 2 CO 3   are dibasic. Their basicity is 2 while   H 3 PO 4   is tribasic, basicity is 3.  When the H +   in an acid is replaced by metallic ions or ammonium ions, a salt is formed  Na +   +   HCl   NaCl   + Cl -  NH 4 +   +   HNO 3   NH 4 NO 3   +   NO 3 -  PROPERTIES OF ACIDS  Physical properties :     Dilute acids have a sour taste (e.g. taste of an unripe fruit).     They turn blue litmus paper red.They are corrosive when concentrated     They are soluble water  Chemical practical:     They give salts,   water and CO 2   gas when they react with carbonate salt (CO 3 2 - ) .     They give salts, water and SO 2   gas when they react with SO 3 2 -   salts     They liberate hydrogen gas when they react with metals higher than hydrogen in the  electrochemical series (e.g. Zn, Fe, Na,   etc)     They undergo neutralization reaction .That is, they react with bases to give salt and water  only.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   145  BASES AND   ALKALIS  Most oxides and hydroxides of metals are bases e.g. KOH, MgO, CuO, Na 2 O etc.  Most of them are insoluble in water.  However,those   of them that are soluble in water are called alkalis  Thus, an alkali is a soluble base (hydroxide).  NaOH and KOH   are regarded as strong alkalis because they ionize completely in water  Ca(OH) 2   and NH 4 OH ( also known as aquous ammonia)   are regarded as   weak   alkalis  because they   ionize partially in water.  In fact, all alkalis are bases, but all bases are not alkalis.  PROPERTIES OF ALKALIS/BASES  Physical properties:     Alkalis or bases have bitter taste.     They are soapy when touched     They   turn red litmus paper blue.     When they are concentrated, they are corrosive.  Chemical properties :     They undergo neutralization reaction with acids to form salt and water only     When they react with ammonium salts in the presence of heat, they give salts, water   and  ammonia gas.  NOTE:  (i)   Caustic Soda   (NaOH) is   deliquescent and attacks glass.  (ii)   Soda lime   is quicklime ( CaO ) slaked with   caustic   soda   (NaOH).  It is not deliquescent and does not attack glass.  This is very useful during the laboratory prepara tion of methane  SALTS  A salt is the compound formed when all or part of the ionizable hydrogen of an acid is  replaced by metallic ions or ammonium ions.  TYPES OF SALTS  NORMAL SALTS  This is formed when   ALL   the hydrogen are replaced by   metals e.g.  H 2 SO 4 (aq)   +   2 NaOH (aq)   Na 2 SO   4(aq)   + 2 H 2 O (l)  No ionizable hydrogen can be found in the above compounds.  This shows that all the   hydrogen ions are replaced.  T hey are neutral to litmus. Some,   however ,   will undergo hydrolysis in water to give an acidic or  alkaline solution. Na 2 CO 3 , AICI 3 , NaCl etc.  a)   ACID SALTS  This is when the ionizable hydrogen ions of an acid are partially replaced   –   that is, not  completely replaced by metals.Hydrogen is always present   in their compounds.  e.g. NaHCO 3 , NaHSO 4   NaHS etc  H 2 SO 4 (aq)   + NaOH (aq)   NaHSO   4(aq)   +H 2 O (l)

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   146  An acid salt still contains replaceable H +   and has acidic properties.  For example, it will turn litmus paper from blue to red etc.  It will undergo   further neutralization   reaction to form a normal salt.  NaHSO 4(aq) +NaOH   (aq)   Na 2 SO 4 (aq)   + H 2 O   (l)  b)   BASIC SALT  During neutralization, if the   acid is not sufficient to neutralize the base, a basic salt is  formed.  They contain the hydroxide ion,   (OH - ).However, with more acid,   the reaction goes to  completion forming normal salt.  Do bear in mind that as a basic salt, it will have all the propert ies of a base.  Zn(OH)Cl + HCl (aq)   ZnCl 2   +H 2 O   (l)  basic salt   acid   normal salt water  c)   DOUBLE SALTS  They produce three different ions in solution. Two of   these ions are positively charged, while  the other is negatively charged.  The two positively charged ions could be metallic or ammonium ions or a combination of both  metallic or ammonium ions.  e.g.(NH 4 ) 2 Fe(SO 4 ) 2. 6H 2 O, KAI(SO 4 ) 2. 12H 2 O(potash alum) etc.  d)   C OMPLEX SALTS  These contain complex ions, that is, ions consisting of charged group of atoms e.g.  Na 2 Zn(OH) 4   2Na +   +   [Zn(OH) 4 ] 2 -  charged group  NaAI (OH) 4   Na +   +   [AI(OH) 4 ] -  charged group  PREPARATION OF SALTS  Salt can be classified   (in terms of solubility in water)   into   soluble and insoluble salts.  The method or   conditions used in preparing any salt depend largely on:  (i)   The solubility of   the   salt in water.  (ii)   The stability of   the salt to heat.  The following methods could be used in preparing soluble salts  (1)   Neutralization  (2)   Dilute acid and metal  (3)   Dilute acid and trixoca rbonate (IV)  These are also the three chemical properties of acids. They produce soluble salts  only

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   147  RECOVERY OF SOLUBLE SALT FROM SOLUTION  In all cases, water is always produced along with the salt. To recover the salts, two methods are  considered.  Evaporation to dryness  Crystallization  Evaporation   is used if the salt can withstand dry heating e.g. most chlorides.  e.g. NaCl,KCl,CaCl 2   etc.  Crystallization is used if the salt   decompose   on   heating   e.g. all NO 3   salt, F eSO 4 ,CuSO 4   etc.  INSOLUBLE SALTS:   Two method are used in preparing them  (1)   Double decomposition  This has to do with the exchange of radicals. The reactants are both soluble. One of the  products is insoluble while the other is insoluble  AgNO 3(aq)   +   NaCl (aq)   AgCl (s) +NaNO 3(aq)  soluble   soluble   insoluble   soluble  BaCl 2 + K 2 SO 4   BaSO 4(S)   +   2KCI (aq)  soluble   soluble   insoluble   soluble  (white ppt)  (2)   Combination of constituent element  This involves a direct combination of two elements to form the insoluble salts.  e.g.   Fe (s)   +CI 2(g)   FeS (s)  2Fe (s)   +Cl 2(g)   2FeCl 3(S)  TAKE NOTE!  An   anhydrous salt   is a salt without water of crystallization .It is usually prepared in the  absence of water. E.g. Na 2 CO 3  (1)   A hydrated salt   is a salt which contains water of crystallization.E.g. Na 2 CO 3 .10H 2 O  (2)   Amorphous   means shapeless, the opposite of amorphou s is crystalline. So another name  for an amorphous substance is non - crystalline substance.  ATOM I CITY  This is the number of atom in a molecule of an element e.g.  (1)   Monatomic molecules  They have atomicity of   one e.g.  All the noble gases (Helium, Neon, Argon) etc  (2)   D iatomic molecules  They have atomicity of two e.g. O 2 , H 2 ,N 2   and   all the halogens (F 2 ,CL 2 , Br 2 , L 2 ) etc  (3)   Polyatomic molecules  They have three or more atoms in their molecules  Ozone has atomicity of   3  phosphorus (P 4 )   has   4  and Sulphur (S 8 ) has   8  There are largely two kinds of molecules

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   148  Molecule of an element  This is formed when atoms of the same element combine  H + H   H 2  in molecule of an element , no new substance is formed  In other words, the product is the same as the reactants  Molecule of a compound  This is formed when atoms of different elements combine  2H 2   +O 2   2H 2 O  A new substance is formed in a molecule of a compound.  H 2 O is   different from both hydrogen and oxygen   unlike molecule of an element   where  the product is the same as the reactants

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   149  MOLE CONCEPT  A woman selling uncooked rice at the street in Lagos will use either a milk cup or a derica  cup to make measurements.  Isn’t it?  Of course, yes!  Good!!  In Chemistry,  w e have one major cup for measurement. It is called THE MOLE  WHAT A MILK CUP IS TO A RICE SELLER IS WHAT MOLE IS TO A  CHEMIST!  We use mole to make measurements of particles.  The particles are also called elementary entities.  These particles are atoms, molecules,   ions, sub atomic particles  (protons, electrons and neutrons) etc.  More so, in the same way you cannot call the milk cup rice, you cannot call a  mole a particle  Definition  The mole is the amount of substance which   contain as many elementary  entitles (or particles) as there are carbon atoms in 12g of carbon   –   12   isotopes  Further explanation  1 mole of carbon   is the   number of atoms   in exactly 12g of the carbon - 12 isotope.  And since 12g is the RAM of carbon in   grammes,  Therefore, we can conclude at this point that :  1 mole of   12 C=12g=Ram of carbon 12 in grammes  More so, always remember, one mole is the same thing as one molar mass  1 mole of   12 C=12g=Ram of carbon 12 in grammes = molar mass of   carbon  One mole of Carbon = molar mass of Carbon  And if this is true for carbon, then it is true for all elements.  Thus,  .:   1 MOLE=MOLAR MASS ( And this is true for all element)  Similarly , One mole is also equal to 6.02   X 10 23   particles .  This number is the Avogadro Number (N).  1 MOLE=AVOGADRO’S NUMBER= 6.02   x 10 23   particles  T he mole is very useful concept since a single atom or molecule is extremely small and  cannot be se en or weighed, but one mole of   an   atom or molecule can be seen, and   can be  weighed.

One mole =atomic mass of an element (in grammes)  2.   One mole = 6.02x10 23   particles or Avogadro Number ( N )  3.   One mole = molar   volume of gas at s. t. p which is 22.4dm 3  4.   One mole = Relative molecular mass of molecules or compounds (in grams)  5.   One mole =   one faraday of   electricity for a univalent ion which is 96, 500 coulombs  6.   One mole = molar mass of elements or compounds  Never f orget that each time rela tive molecular mass or relative   atomic mass or  formula mass is writtren in grammes, it is called molar mass.  Okay? Good !  GRASP THIS!  (1)   Molar mass is calculated in the gramme per mole (gmol - 1 )  or simply in grammes (g)  (2)   Relative molecular mass (RMM) or formula mass has no unit  (3)   Relative atomic mass has no unit  R.M.M of a gas =2 x vapour density  The molar mass (i.e. mass of one mole) of sodium is 23g/mol but the relative   atomic mass of  sodium is 23 (no unit).  The RMM of NaCl is   23 + 35.5 = 58.5  REASON!  The relative atomic mass and the relative molecular mass do not have   unit s   because they  express ratio (not the actual mass).  That is, it is just the number of times a n atom or molecule of an element or a compound is  heavier than one - twelfth (1/12) the mass of one atom of carbon 12 isotope. ( 12 C).  However, whenever it is expressed in grammes, it is called molar mass.  -  -   Shhhh!   DID YOU ATTEND PRIMARY SCHOOL?  -  -   Do you still remember that 10mm makes 1cm?  -   Yesssss! ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   152  ATOM , MOLECULE OR GAS   AND MOLAR VOLUME (EXPLANATION)  Mr Ejay :   One mole of   oxygen   atom   is equal to   what?  Student:   16g!  Mr Ejay : Why?  Student: An atom is   involved!  Mr Ejay :Very well!  Next question,  Mr Ejay : One mole of   oxygen gas   will be   what?  Student: 16g!  Mr Ejay : Oh no!The answer is   32g  Recall that it is not an atom but a gas or you call it oxygen molecule.  Therefore, (1 mole of oxygen gas or molecule O 2 ) = 2 x 16 = 32g.  One mole of   a gas or   a molecule of an element = 2 x relative atomic mass of the  element in grammes (molar mass).  It is this one mole of oxygen molecule that contains 22.4dm 3   at stp.  1 mole of oxygen gas (O 2 )   = 2 x RAM= 22.4 dm 3   at STP.  Mola r mass is the mass of one mole   of either an element or a compound.  That means, we can use it for both elements and   compounds instead of relative atomic mass  (element) or relative molecular mass (molecules and compounds).  More so,  If   1 mole   = molar mass  Then, ½ mole = ½ of molar mass  Also, 0.2 mole = 0.2 of molar mass  EXAMPLE  Molar   mass of   sodium (Na) = 23g/mol.= or simply 23g  1.   1 mole of Na   = molar mass of Na = (1 x 23) g/mol.  2.   ½ mole of Na   =   ½ x 23   = 11.5g  3.   0.2 mole of Na   =   0.2 x 23 =   4.6g  2.0   moles of Na   =   2 x 23   =   46g  Only   1 mole   has the unit   g/mol   while the rest are expressed in   grammes .  Why?  Because they are not molar masses.  They are call reacting masses  Molar mass, once again, is the mass of 1 mole.
