The stoichiometry of a reaction shows the relationship between the amount of reactant   that  reacted   and   the product formed. It is often expressed in mole ratio.  NOTE:  Values expressing   ratio   do   not   have units because they do not express   actual value s .  This is why relative atomic mass   (or RAM) , relative molecular mass   (or RMM) , formula mass,  mole ratio   do not have   units.  PAY ATTENTION TO THESE QUESTIONS !  Question 1  Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide formed when 3g of magnesium are burned in oxygen  (0=16; Mg =24)  SOLUTION :   3g of Mg is given and we are calculating for mass  Method:   Mass to mass   relationship  Equation   2Mg (s)   + O 2(g)   2MgO (s)  Moles from equation   2   :   1   2  Mole ratio   :   2   :   1   2  Molar mass   :   (24g)   :   (2x16) g   (24+16) g  24g   32g   40g  Equation mass :   2   x   24   1 x 32g   2   x   40  48g   32g   80g  Remember that     molar mass is the mass of one mole.     a nd the molar mass of diatomic molecule is 2 x RAM  From the   equation above :   48g of Mg   formed 80g of MgO   (equation)  From   the question asked :   3g of Mg will form   𝒙   of MgO   (question)  Cross multiply  3   ×   80   =   48 𝑥  𝑥   =   3   ×   80  48   =   5 𝑔  Hint: The idea is to stay with what we are given and what we are   looking for

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   165  LIMITING AND EXCESS REAGENTS  During a chemical reaction of two substances, one of the reactants gets used up while the other  is stilling remaining.  The one that get used up is called the limiting reagent because it determines the actual amount  of product possible at that very moment.  It is the limiting regeant that actually ends the reaction.  The other reactant which has not been used as at the time the reaction ends is called the excess  regeant.  There are different ways of calculating the limiting and the excess regeants.  Metho d 1: mass of product produced.  The reactant that produced the greater amount of product is the one in excess . Thus,it   will be  the excess regeant.  The reactant with a less amount of product is the limiting reagent.  Method 2: Mole ratio comparison  Compare the   mole ratio of the reactants   in the question   given with the   mole ratio of the  reactants   in the equation   of the reaction.  If the mole of a reactant in the question is greater than its   mole in the equation , that  reactant is the excess reagent. If   it is less, then, it is the limiting reagent.  NOTE:  (1)   Always use the limiting reagent for your calculations.  (2)   You will know you are dealing with limiting and excess reagents when the values of the  two reactants are given instead of one of them  EXAMPLE 1  (a) What is the mass of the oxide formed when 2g of lithium is burnt in 3g of oxygen?  (b)   What is the mass of the oxide formed when lithium is burnt in   4 g of oxygen?  SOLUTION   (a)  As you can see, we are given the masses of the two reactants  Mass   of Lethium= 2g  Mass of oxygen gas= 3g  If you check the previous examples, you will notice that only the value of one of the reactants is  always given.

Do not forget that volumetric or quantitative analysis has to do  with measurements. In fact, it is a measurement of volumes and masses precisely.  Titration is the method used in volumetric analysis, in which a solution from a burette (acid)  is added to a known volume of a second solution (base) in a conical flask until the reaction is  complete as shown by a sudden change in the colour of indicator   used.  Indicator   PH range   Acid   Base   End - point   titration  Litmus   5.0 - 8.0   red   Blue   purple   SA & SB  Methyl orange   2.9 - 4.6   pink   yellow   orange   SA & WB or   SA  & CO 3 2 -   salts  Phenolphthalein   8.3 - 10.0   colourless   Pink   colourless   SB &WA  Methyl red   4.4 - 6.3   red   yellow   orange   SA & SB  SA & SB=   strong acid and base   WA & W B   mean weak k acid and base respectively  - The pipette is used in measuring a fixed volume of the base. Most times , voume of 20 cm 3   or  25cm 3   is used .  - The titration is often done up to three times after which the average volume of acid used could  be determined.  - Volumes within the range of   ± 0.2   only are considered   when calculating   average titre value of  acids   used .

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   176  PROCEDURE DURING TITRATION  (1)   Pipette 20cm 3   of an alkali (base) into a clean conical flask, and add 2 or 3 drops of the  indicators you want to use.  (2)   Fill the burette with the acid using a funnel if you like. Release some o f the acid solution  through the tap in order to expel air bubbles, after then take your initial burette reading  (3)   Place the conical flask on a white paper or a white tile under the burette to know   easily  when the end point is reached  (4)   Titrate by releasing   the acid solution through the tap; use one hand to control the tap  and use the other hand to shake the flask constantly to ensure a uniform reaction or  mixture  (5)   Keep adding the acid and shaking simultaneously until there is a change in the colour of  th e indicator.  (6)   At the end point, r ecord the final burette reading.  The volume of the acid used equa ls final burette value minus   the initial burette value.  This is the first titration or titre value  (7)   Repeat   the procedure two more times to obta in the average volume of acid used.  .   Do not forget to record the size of pipette or the volume of the bade used  PRECAUTIONS DURING TITRATION  (1)   Rinse the burette and the pipette   with the solution to be used in them (after washing  with water) to avoid diluting the solutions with the remains of water in them.  (2)   Air bubbles should be removed from the burette and pipette, to obtain accurate volume  of the solutions.  (3)   Never rinse the tit ration flash with the solution it is to hold, to avoid using more or less  than the required volume. The solution   become s   diluted.  The initial concentration will be higher than the new (or final) concentration.  However, the amount of moles or reacting mass wi ll not change.  I f there is 5g of   salt in a pot of soup, adding more water to the soup will not add or reduce  the 5g of salt in the soup.  Thus  Number of moles or mass of the of the initial   =   Number of moles or mass   of the  concentration   final concentration  n 1 = n 2   m 1 = m 2  Dilution always affects concentration of a solution.  Once water is added to a solution, new concentration will be produced.  However, the mass or mole of solute will not change.  The initial concentration will be higher than the new (or final) concentration.  Assuming you put 10g of sugar in a cup containin g 20cm 3   of water and after a  while, you added more water of 5cm 3 , what will happen?  The taste will change. It will taste less sugary, right?  This means. The concentration has changed.  In other words, the concentration will reduce.  𝒄𝟏   ≠   𝒄𝟐   𝒑𝟏   ≠   𝒑𝟐   but n1=n2 and m1=m2  If the volume of water in a sugar solution changes   from 20cm 3   to 25cm 3 , the volume of the  solvent will change but the solute will not change.  The solute = to the amount of sugar in the solution. It will still remain 10g .This means the solute  is the only thing that will not change . Volume or solvent is i n cm 3   or dm 3   while the solute is in  moles or grammes  Initial mass of sugar (or solute) in 20cm 3   of the solvent= final mass of sugar (solute) in the  25cm 3   of the solvent  Solute can be expressed in mole(n) or mass(m).Therefore, if we express the solute   in mole,  Initial moles= final moles(n 1   = n 2 ).And if we express the solute in mass,  Initial mass= final mass(m 1 =m 2 )  This is the whole idea behind the calcution involving dilution principle. ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   188  PRIMARY AND SECONDARY STANDARDS &   STOCK SOLUTION  PRIMARY STANDARDS   are reagents that their standard solutions can be prepared directly  because they are very p ure, stable, not hygroscopic, have   a high molecular mass es and soluble in  water or in a   given solvent .  They are non - toxic, inexpensive and readily available.  They are often used to prepare secondary standards.  SECONDARY STANDARDS   are s olutions obtained by standardizing   them against primary  standards.  Oxalic acid is used to standardize NaOH. The oxalic   acid is the primary standard while the  NaOH is the secondary standard.  NOTE:     NaOH and KOH are deliquescent substances. They have to be standardize with oxalic acid  after preparations.     Concentrated H 2 SO 4   is hygroscopic and HCl and HNO 3   are volat ile. They   are standardize  with   Na 2 CO 3  NaCl is usually used to standardize AgNO 3  K 2 Cr 2 O 7   is used to stardardize redox reactions  A   stock solution   is a concentrated   solution   that will be diluted to some lower concentration for  actual use. They help us to save a lot of time, reduce storage space and conserve materials.  They include Strong acids and strong alkalis which have already been standardize with other  substances   becaus e of the difficulty and inaccuracy in preparing their standard solutions directly.  They are usually standardize with Na 2 CO 3   or oxalic acid (H 2 C 2 O 4 ). ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   240  SOLUBILITY  The solubility of a solute in a solvent at a given temperature is the number of mole s   of  the solute that will saturate 1dm 3   of the solvent at that temperature .  It can be   expressed in mole per dm 3   or gramme per dm 3   or even in gramme per 100g  or gramme per 1000g  A saturated solution of a solute at a particular temperature is one which contains as  much solute as it can dissolve at that temperature in the presence of   undisso lved  solute.  A supersaturated solution is one which dissolve more of the solute than it can normally  dissolve at that temperature .  A supersaturated solution is not stable.  Any rough treatment of the solution will crystallize the extra solute it disso lved.  The solubility of gases generally decreases with a rise in temperature, while that of most  solid solutes increases, EXCEPT for Ca(OH) 2   and CaSO 4.  W hile   pressure affects the solubility of gases, it does not have any effect on the solubility  of solid   solutes  EXAMPLE 1  Calculate the solubility of the following in  (i)   gdm − 3   (ii)   moldm − 3   at room temperature  . An unsaturated solution is like ‘ a hungry man’ .  Thus, the evidence that a solution is   saturated is that it has undissolved solute.  The solubility product is the   equilibrium constant for the equilibrium between an  undissolved salt and its ions in a saturated solution.  A solubility product is generally used for sparingly soluble salts e. gAgCl  𝐴𝑔𝐶𝑙 ( 𝑠 )   ⇌   𝐴𝑔 ( 𝑎𝑞 )  +   +   𝐶𝑙 ( 𝑎𝑞 )  −  By applying equilibrium law ,  𝐾   =   [ 𝐴𝑔 ( 𝑎𝑞 )  +   ] [ 𝐶𝑙 ( 𝑎𝑞 )  −   ]  [ 𝐴𝑔 ( 𝑠 ) ]  [ 𝐴𝑔𝐶𝑙 ( 𝑠 ) ]   =   1  Concentration of pure solid is constant. All elements in group 1 have valency of  +1  e.g.   𝑵𝒂 +   , 𝑲 +   ,   𝑯 +   ,  2.   All elements in group 2 have   valency of  +2  e.g.   𝑴𝒈 𝟐 + 𝑪𝒂 𝟐 +   , 𝑩𝒂 𝟐 +  3.   All elements in group 3 have valency of  +3  e.g.   𝑨𝒍 𝟑 +  4.   All elements in group 6 have valency of  6 - 8=   - 2  e.g.   𝑶 𝟐 −   , 𝑺 𝟐 −  5.   All elements in group 7 have valency of  7 - 8=   - 1  e.g.   𝑭 −   ,   𝑪𝒍 −  6. The oxidation number of an element in uncombined form equals zero  (e.g.   𝑯 𝟐  𝟎 ,   𝑶 𝟐  𝟎 , 𝑵𝒂 𝟎   etc)  2.   The   sum of the oxidation number of elements in a compound equals ZERO.  (   e.g. NaCl=0,   CaO=0 ,   H 2 SO 4 =0   etc.)  3.   The oxidation number of an ion equals the charge it carries.  (e.g. S 2 -   = - 2 ,   HCO 3 -   =   - 1   SO 4 2 - = - 2 etc.)  EXAMPLES  1. ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   260  Part   3.   REDOX REACTION  1.   RED = REDUCTION   OX = OXIDATION  REDOX REACTION =   (REDUCTION + OXIDATION)   REACTION  BOTH ARE COMPLEMENTARY REACTIONS.  This means, both of them MUST happen at the same   time.  For the purpose of this lesson, take note of   ‘ RR ’   and   ‘OO’  ‘RR’   means :   R educing agent and   R eduction.  A substance cannot have   ‘RR’   in the ame reaction.  In other words, i f a substance is a   Reducing agent   ( R )   , then it cannot undergo  Reduction(R ) in the same reaction or at the same time.  Similarly,   ‘OO’   means:   O xidizing agent and   O xidation  A substance cannot have   ‘ OO ’   in the ame reaction.  In other words, i f a substance is a n   Oxidizing   agent   ( O )   , then ,   it cannot undergo  OXIDATION (O ) in the same reaction or at the same time.  ‘ RR’   must not go together. A nd   ‘OO’   must not go together.  Hints : you cannot be the giver and the receiver at the same time  Thus ,   R EDUCING AGENTS undergo   O XIDATION e.g. METALS   𝑅   →   𝑂  .   O XIDIZING AGENTS undergo   R EDUCTION e.g. NON METALS   𝑂   →   𝑅  Let’s examine the c ommonest definition   for redox     Oxidation is the addition of oxygen or the removal of hydrogen.     Reduction is the addition of hydrogen or the removal of oxygen.  Note:   The reducing agent and the oxidizing agent are both   REACTANTS .  They are   NOT PRODUCTS . Never forget that!  A   +   BO   AO   +   B  I n the equation above , ‘ O’   is oxygen while ‘ A   and   B ’ are unknown elements.  ‘A   and   BO’   are the reactants. They form the reducing and oxidizing agents.  ‘ AO   and   B ’   are the products. They cannot be the oxidizing and the reducing agent s .  1.   However,   from   the   product side ,   we can   tell which of the reactants   is undergoing oxidation  or reduction .  A   +   BO   AO   +   B  From the product side,   A   has become   AO.   (It has gained oxygen).That is oxidation.  Therefore   A   is the reducing agent.  BO , on the other hand,   has become   B . (It has lost oxygen) .   That is reduction.  Therefore   BO   is the oxidizing agent.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   261  FACTS ABOUT REDOX REACTION S  NON -   METALS   METALS  1   They ionize or become ion by electron  gain.  They ionize or become ion by electron   loss.  2   They are called   electron acceptors   They are called   electron donnors  3   Gain of electrons makes them negatively  charged ( R eduction). O 2 -   , Cl -   , S 2 -   ( R )  Loss of elections makes them positively charged  ( O xidation). H + , Na +   , Mg 2+   (O)  4   They are   therefore   oxidizing agents   (O)   They are reducing agents .   ( R )  5   They are anions   They are cations  6   They are electronegative elements   They are electropositive elements  7   Examples include O 2   , Cl 2   S etc   Examples include, H 2   , Na , K etc  8   The addition of   oxygen or   a non metal is  oxidation .  In other words:  Any marriage to non metal will produce  oxidation.   Why?  Non m etals are oxidizing agents.  Their job is to produce oxidation  The addition of   hydrogen or   a metal is  reduction.  In other words :  Any marriage to a metal will produce  reduction.   Why?  Metals are reducing agents .  Their job is to produce reduction.  9   The removal of   oxygen or a   non - metal  means oxidation CANNOT happen.  In other words, the removal of   a non  metal will produce   reduction.  The removal of   hydrogen or a metal means  reduction CANNOT happen.  In other words, the removal of metals means  oxidation.  10   BY definition , Oxidation is the addition  of oxygen .  Oxygen = non metal  Therefore ,  Oxidation is   the addition of a non   –  metal like oxygen or electronegative  element, or anion or oxidizing agent or  electron acceptor  BY definition , Reduction is the addition of  hydrogen .  Hydrogen = metal  Therefore ,  Reduction is the addition of a metal like  hydrogen or   electropositive element, or cation  or reducing agent or electron donor

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   262  Other descriptions of metals and non metals  NON -   METALS   METALS  1   Most e lectronegative   Most e lectropositive  2   Least   electropositive.   L east electronegative  3   Most o xidizing   agents   Most r educing   agents  4   L east reducing   L east oxidizing  Note,   elect ronegative, electropositive , oxidizing and reducing   are characteristics which  can be used for metals and non metals.  1.   A reaction of Na and Cl 2     Na   is metal while   Cl 2   is a non   -   metal  Na   is electropositive while Cl 2   is electronegative.     This means, in a reaction involving   Na and Cl 2  Na   will function as a metal while Cl 2   will function as a non   -   metal.  Most redox questions are in the form above but a few are different.  2.   A reaction of F 2   and Cl 2     F 2   and Cl 2   are both non -  metals.     Both are electronegative  elements     But F 2   is more reactive than Cl 2  This means F 2   is more electronegative  than Cl 2   .     This means, in a reaction  involving F 2   and Cl 2 ,  F 2   will function as a non metal  while Cl 2   will function as a  metal.     F 2   is more electronegative would also  mean:  I t is more oxidizing.  I t is less electropositive.  I t is less reducing .  On the other hand     Cl 2   is less electronegative would also  mean:  I t is   less oxidizing  I t is   more   electropositive.  I t is more reducing.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   263  3.   A reaction of Na and Cu     Na   and   Cu   are both metals.     Both are electropositive elements     But   Na   is more reactive than   Cu     This means, in a reaction  involving   Na   and   Cu ,  Na   will function as a   metal while  Cu   will function as a non - metal.     Na   is more electro positive   would also  mean:  It is mo re   reducing .  It is less   electronegative .  It is less oxidizing  On the other hand     Cu   is less electro positive   would also  mean:  It is   less reducing  It is   more   electro negative  It is more oxiding  FURTHER EXPLANATION  AS A REMINDER ON OXIDATION  Oxidation is the addition of non metal   or the removal of metal  The   following also refer to non metal s :  Oxygen,  electronegative,  oxidizing agent,  electron acceptor,  decrease in oxidation number  least electropositive  least reducing  Where two metals are given, the less electropositive   substance is treated as a  non metal.  Where two reducing agents are involved, the less reducing agent s   is treated as  a non metal.  Oxidation always occurs at the ANODE

With the above concept, you can tell which non metal is more reactive   than the other.  For example:  1.   Oxygen is more reactive or more oxidizing or more electronegative than bromine.  2.   Or we can say, bromine is less reactive, less oxiding or less electronegative than oxygen.  3.   Or bromine is less reactive , more reducing or more e lectropositive than oxygen.  The concept above shows, fluorine is the most electronegative element while   phosphorus is the  least.  In other words, fluorine   is   the most oxidizing non - metal   while phosphorus is the least.  Note less or more is for 2   elements or substances  Least or most is for 3 or more elements or substances  USEFUL CONCEPT 2  O h   I   B ring   C hemistry   N ote   S ir   F orget … REPRESENTS  𝑶𝑯 −   𝑰 −   𝑩𝒓 −   𝑪𝒍 −   𝑵𝑶 𝟑  −   𝑺𝑶 𝟒  𝟐 −   𝑭 −  electronegativity increases  This is most useful in electrolysis.  𝐹 −   𝑖𝑠   𝑡 ℎ 𝑒   𝑚𝑜𝑠𝑡   𝑒𝑙𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑛𝑒𝑔𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑣𝑒   𝑜𝑟   𝑚𝑜𝑠𝑡   𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑣𝑒   𝑎𝑛𝑖𝑜𝑛   ( 𝑛𝑜𝑛   𝑚 𝑒𝑡𝑎𝑙 )   𝑤 ℎ 𝑖𝑙𝑒   𝑂𝐻 −   𝑖𝑠   𝑡 ℎ 𝑒   𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑡  SO 4 2 -   is more reactive than OH -   .  In the electrolysis of concentrated H 2 SO 4 , for example, OH -   is preferentially discharge as  oxygen gas while SO 4 2 -   remains in the solution.

The following also refer to metal s :  Hydrogen,  electropositive ,  reducing agent,  electron donor,  increase in oxidation number  Least electronegative  Least oxidizing     Where two non   metals are given, the less electronegative element is  treated as a metal.     Where two oxidizing agents are involved, the less oxidizing agent is  treated as a metal.  Reduction always occurs at the cathode  Electrochemical series of metals  P eter   S amuel   C an   M ake   A   Z oo   I n   T own   L agos   H owever   C ommon   M en   A re   A round. ..  K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au  From the most reactive to   the least reactive  This means, potassium(K) is the most reactive metal while gold is the least  reactive (Au)  K is the most electropositive element while gold is the the least  QUESTIONS  1.   If   K is the   most electropositive metal , can we also say it is the   least electronegative  metal?  YES , OF COURSE!  2.   Most electronegative element   also means least electropositive element.  True or false?  Answer:   TRUE  3.   Most reducing agent also means least oxidizing.  True or false?  Answer :   TRUE

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   285  ELECTROCHEMISTRY  Electrochemistry   involves the transfer of ele ctrons from one chemical specie   to another.  This is what happen s   in a redox reaction.   Thus , electrochemistry deals with two types of   cells.  2.   Electrochemical cells  3.   Electrolytic cells (OR   electrolysis)  Note:   Both involves redox reaction s  In both electrochemical   reaction   and electrolysis, oxidation occurs at the anode  while reduction occurs at the cathode  INTRODUCTION TO ELECTROCHEMICAL CELL  Have you seen a battery before?  What you call   battery is actually called a cell in Chemistry or Physics.  The electrochemical cell is   generally called ‘battery’. In c hemistry,   however, ‘one battery’ is  actually called a cell while two or more cells are called battery.  Electrode potential  Electrode + potential = Electrode potential  Electrode   is an y   material which can   conductor   electricity .  They are basically metal s. However,   graphite which is a non metal is also used as an electrode.  By the way, graphite is the only non   – metal which can   conduct electricity.  Potential   simply means voltage.  Electrode potential simply means voltage produced by a metal when it comes in  contact with a solution of its own salt.  The electrode potentials are written in half - cells. Thus, a cell involves two   half cells. One is  oxidation half cell and the other is reduction half cell.  Note: There are two types of electrochemical cells:  Primary cells:  They are not rechargeable once used up .   e.g .   Daniel   cell, Lechlanche   etc.  Secondary   cells:  They are rechargea ble .   e.g .   car battery, Nife cell etc.  The secondary cells are recharged by electrolysis while the primary cells are not  rechargeable once used up.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   286  TEN   FACTS YOU MUST KNOW ABOUT   ELECTROCHEMICAL CELL  1.   Each time a metal comes in contact with a solution containing its own salt, an  electrode potential is formed. This means voltage is   produced.  2.   This electrode poten tial cannot be measure directly .  Why?  This is because every attempt to measure it wi ll   introduce another   electrode  potential.  What then are we going to do?  We have to keep the value of one of the metals constant.  3.   Thus,   Hydrogen   is made to have an assumed electrode potential value of   zero under  certain conditions.This   is called standard hydrogen potential.  Then after, the half cell of hydrog en is compared   with that of other metals through a  salt bridge.  This   is how the voltage of each metal was   determined.  In any case,   because the values   of the metals were   obtained   under certa in conditions,  they are called   standard electrode potential (SEP)   instead of electrode  potential .  The standard conditions are :  Concentration of solution   1 mole dm   - 3  Temperature   25 o c  Pressure   l atmosphere  Thus, while we cannot measure electrode potential, standard electrode potential can  .   be measured.  Then what next?  After then, the various   standard   electrode   potential   ( SEP )   values   obtained   were  arranged from   lowest to   highest value   down wards .  This is how electrochemical series of metal is obtained   which can   also be called  activity series   of metals  4.   From the electrochemical series, the   EMF of an elec trochemical cell   (or battery) can  be   calculated.  In an electrochemical cell   –   the more reactive metal forms the   ANODE while the less  reactive   metal forms the CATHODE.  This means in electrochemical cell, the anode is negative while the cathode  is positive .

IN SUMMARY     The electrochemical series   , or reactivity series is a list of elements in the  order of their reducing   power on increasing SEP.     An element higher in the series will   displace a lower element from   its  solution e.g.  𝒁𝒏 ( 𝒔 )   +   𝑪𝒖𝑪 𝒍 𝟐 ( 𝒂𝒒 )   →   𝒁𝒏𝑪 𝒍 𝟐 ( 𝒂𝒒 )   +   𝑪𝒖 ( 𝒔 )     A cell is made up of two half -   cells :   o xidation and   r eduction half - cells     The standard hydroge n electrode, S.H. E is   defined to have an EMF of  0.000V     A standard electrode potential is measured with the SHE as the left -   hand  half cell     The more negative electrode should be the left - hand half - cell     The more negative half   - cell gives up electrons to the   external circuit.     The cell e.m.f is given by :  𝑬 𝒄𝒆𝒍𝒍   =   𝑬 𝒄𝒂𝒕𝒉𝒐𝒅𝒆   −   𝑬 𝒂𝒏𝒐𝒅𝒆  𝑬 𝒄𝒆𝒍𝒍   =   𝑬 𝒓𝒊𝒈𝒉𝒕   −   𝑬 𝒍𝒆𝒇𝒕     Metals with the most negative electrode potential are the best reducing  agent     The negative half   - cell has the higher   concentration .  Note:   There are two types of electrochemical cells:  Primary cells:   They are not rechargeable once used up  e.g .   Daniel cell, Lechlanche etc.  Secondary cells:  They are rechargeable.e.g car battery, Nife cell etc.  The   secondary cell s are recharged by electrolysis .

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   291  ELECTROLYSIS  This is a chemical decomposition of an electrolyte in aqueous or molten form by the passage of  a direct current.  The anode is the   positive   elec trode while the cathode is the   negative electrode.  Generally, during electrolysis,   the less reactive ion is always   preferentially discharged.  Using the electrochemical series, we can easily know the more reactive metals and non -   metals.  There are four factors which affect the discharge of ion during elec trolysis  1.   Position of the ion in the electrochemical series  2.   Concentration of the ions  3.   Nature of electrode  4.   Ion - electrode agreement  Factor 1: Position of the ion in the electrochemical series  Factor 1   is a general factor while   factor 2 to 4   are exceptional.  According to   Factor 1 , weaker ions are discharged as atoms or molecules while the stronger  ions remain in the solution.  Factor 2:   Concentration of the ions  Always consider concentration before nature of electrode .  Concentration must be considered only if the two ions going to the same electrode are close in  the electrochemical series.     If the two ions are close, the stronger   ion   is discharged while the  weaker ion remains in the solution.  For example     Cl -   and OH -   are   close, so Cl -   is   always   discharged as Cl 2     H +   and Cu 2+   are close, so H +   is discharged as H 2  Factor 3 :   Nature of electrode     Where Graphite is used, it makes OH -   to be discharged as O 2     Where Platinum is used, it makes Cl -   to be discharged as C l 2     Where mercury is used, it makes Na +   to be discharged as   Na  NOTE:   Concentration , however, always   over rules nature of electrode .  So where concentration is involved, nature of   electrode is only considered if the  concentration has no effect.  However factor   4   (Ion - electrode agreement) , over rules every other factor  For example, if the electrolyte is a copper salt and the cathode is copper, the copper will be  discharged.  If the ele ctrolyte is a copper salt and the anode   and the cathode   are   copper, the copper   will be  discharged at both the anode and the cathode.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  AN EXCEPTIONAL CHEMISTRY MATERIAL YOU NEED!   304  SECOND LAW OF FARADAY  When the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytes  the relative number of moles of each ion discharged is inversely proportional  to the charge on the ion  NOTE  For 2 nd   law of Faraday to be valid,  1.   two or more electrolytes must b e involved  2.   the two or more electrolytes must receive the same quantity of elecricity ( q ).  In other words the   q   for each of the ions must be the same  LET ’S   PARAPHRASE THE 2 ND   LAW OF FARADAY  The 2 nd   law of Faraday is simply says ,  the ion with the highest valency will have the lowest mole deposition;  while th e ion with the lowest valency   will have the highest mole deposition.  That   is what Michael Faraday mea nt by : ‘ inversely proportional ’ .  However, the product of the mole and   the val ency of one ion deposited must   be equal to the  product of the mole and the valency of the other ion.  If the same   q   is passed through three different  metallic ions :  𝑨 + ,   𝑩 𝟐 +   ,   𝑪 𝟑 +  𝑳𝒆𝒕   𝒂   ,   𝒃   𝒂𝒏𝒅   𝒄   𝒓𝒆𝒑𝒓𝒆𝒔𝒆𝒏𝒕   𝒕𝒉𝒆   𝒎𝒐𝒍𝒆𝒔  𝒐𝒇   𝒆𝒂𝒄𝒉   𝒊𝒐𝒏   𝒅𝒆𝒑𝒐𝒔𝒊𝒕𝒆𝒅   𝒓𝒆𝒔𝒑𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒊𝒗𝒆𝒍𝒚  𝒂   𝑨 + ,   𝒃   𝑩 𝟐 +   𝒄   𝑪 𝟑 +  Then, it follows that after electrolysis, 2 nd   Law  Faraday becomes:  𝑴𝒐𝒍𝒆   ×   𝒗𝒂𝒍𝒆𝒏𝒄𝒚   𝒐𝒇   𝒊𝒐𝒏   =   𝒄𝒐𝒏𝒔𝒕𝒂𝒏𝒕  The valency is the same as the charge on the  ions  𝒂   ×   ( + 𝟏 )   =   𝒃   ×   ( + 𝟐 )   =   𝒄   ×   ( + 𝟑 )  Therefore,   𝒂   =   𝟐𝒃   =   𝟑𝒄  If we make the valency of one of them to  be one, then, the constant equals mole.  Then,   𝒏   =   𝒒  𝒙𝑭  𝟏𝒂   =   𝟐𝒃   =   𝟑𝒄   =   𝒒  𝑭   =   𝒎𝒐𝒍𝒆𝒔   𝒐𝒇   𝑨   𝒅𝒆𝒑𝒐𝒔𝒊𝒕𝒆𝒅  𝟏𝒃   =   𝟏  𝟐   𝒂   =   𝟑  𝟐   𝒄   =   𝒒  𝟐𝑭   =   𝒎𝒐𝒍𝒆𝒔   𝒐𝒇   𝑩   𝒅𝒆𝒑𝒐𝒔𝒊𝒕𝒆𝒅  𝟏   𝒄   =   𝟏  𝟑   𝒂   =   𝟐  𝟑   𝒃   =   𝒒  𝟑𝑭   =   𝒎𝒐𝒍𝒆𝒔   𝒐𝒇   𝑪   𝒅𝒆𝒑𝒐𝒔𝒊𝒕𝒆𝒅  All the formulars are consistent with  𝒏   =   𝒒  𝒙𝑭   𝒘𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒆   𝒙   =   𝒗𝒂𝒍𝒆𝒏𝒄𝒚   𝒐 𝒇   𝒕𝒉𝒆   𝒊𝒐𝒏  To use this formula, however, you must  know the mole of one of them  Where a diatomic molecule is involved, multiply the the mole or the valency by 2. Take note of the phrase:  one mole of the substance.  Standard heat of combustion of graphite or  carbon  1C+O 2   →   CO 2   ( 1 mole of C   )  H 2   + O 2   →   H 2 O   ( 1 mole of H 2 )  C 4 H 10   +   13  2   O 2   →   CO 2   + H 2 O   ( 1 mole of C 4 H 10 )  ∆ 𝐻 𝐶  𝜃   =   ∆ 𝐻 𝑝  𝜃   +   ∆ 𝐻 𝑟  𝜃  The standard enthalpy ( ∆ 𝑯 𝑪  𝜽 ) of an element or  a substance in its free state is zero  THE STANDARD HEAT OF FORMATION  The standard   heat of formation   ( ∆ 𝐻 𝑓  𝜃   ) of a  substance is the heat evolved or absorbed  when   one mole of the substance   is formed from  its elements under standard conditions.  ENDOTHERMIC REACTION  An e ndothermic reaction absorb s   heat from the  environment. It   requires   more energy to break   a  b ond than to form bond it .  EXOTHERMIC REACTION  An exothermic reaction takes   less energy to  break bonds. This is why excess heat is   always  released to the environment. This is  why alkene begins wi th C 2   .  While there is METHANE in an alkane, there is no  METHENE .  So an alkene   has   two carbon atoms carrying a double  bond.  Instead of one carbon atom losing two hydrogen  atoms, the loss is shared between the two carbon  atoms.   Thus, each carbon   atom   with the double  bond loses   a   hydrogen atom. THE FUNCTIONAL GROUP  DEFINATION  The   functional group is an atom ,   a radical  (group of atoms) or a bond common to a  homologus series which determines the main  chemical properties of the series.  NOTE     H ydrocarbons   consist of carbon and hydrogen  only.     They   are generally not very reactive.     Again, the alkyl group being an hydrocarbon,  supports all the general properties of covalent  compounds     More so ,   w hen one hydrogen atom is removed  from   an alkane, what happens? Yes?  An alkyl is formed!     A fter the hydrogen is removed from   an   alkane,  its posi tion is not left vacant .     This means,   another substance must take the  position of the lost hydrogen.     Thus, whatever replaces the lost hydrogen in  an alkane is called   a functional group .  Functional Groups include:  :  CO OH,COO,CONH2,NH2,CO,COH , etc.

In other words,   petrol with octane number of 65% has a mixture of 65% of 2, 2, 4 -   trimethyl  pentane and 35% of heptane.  The more the percentage of the 2, 2, 4   –   trimethyl pentane , the higher the octane number and  the better its quality.  - Petrol with high O.N burns smo othly in internal combustion engines.  Branched   –   chain and cyclic alkanes give petrol samples high O.N.  Tetraethyl lead is added to petrol to prevent knocking; however, it s disadvantage  is that it   causes dizziness and brain damage in children.  1. HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional   chemistry material you probably have not read!   394  FERMENTATION OF STARCH   FERMENTATION OF SUGAR/MOLLASSES  FERMENTATION OF STARCH  Fermentation is a slow decomposition by micro organisms of large molecules  of starch or sugar into smaller molecules such asethanol.  - Malt contain an e nzyme called distase which starch to maltose  - Then after, yeast which contains maltase and zymase is added.  Maltase converts maltose to glucose while the zymase converts glucose to ethanol.  Where ethanol of very high concentration is needed, quicklime   is added to produce rectified  spirit (95% ethanol) and if franctional distillization is incooperated, then, absolute ethanol is  produced.  FERMENTATION OF SUGAR  - Molasses is a syrupy liquid left behind after the crystallization of sugar.  The enzyme invert ase from yeast, converts it to glucose and fructose, which are then  fermented into ethanol by zymase.  - When palm wine stays over night, it changes to alcohol

HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional   chemistry material you probably have not read!   395  POLYMERIZATION  Polymerization   is the linking small molecules called monomers to form bigger molecules  called polymers.  If small molecules are lost in the process, condensation polymerization is formed and  I f nothing is lost, it is addition   polymerization.  The small substances lost can be water , ammonia   etc .  Examples of condensation polymerization are nylon and terylene  Where the monomers are the same, we have copolymer  And if the monomers are different, we have homopolymer  Most polymers ar e formed by   addition polymerization   where no mass is lost in the  formation of the polymer.  Examples are   : polyethene , Perspex , polystyrene  NOTE  1.   FATS AND OILS are large or macro molecules.  However, they are not large enough to be considered as   polymers.  2.   Thermoplastics can be softened by heat and remoulded.  3.   Thermoset cannot be softened by heat or remoulded once they are made  4.   Semi - synthetic polymer like rubber is obtained naturally as a white liquid called latex but  improved artificially .  5.   Natural   rubber is called isoprene or 2 - methyl buta - 1,3 - diene  6.   Artificial or man - made rubber includes neoprene and SBR.  7.   SBR is the most useful. It is used for vehicle tyres and footwear.  It has high resistance to abrasion

HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional   chemistry material you probably have not read!   407  Let us   consider methane again.  In the above chart, there is no substituent.  All the hydrogen atoms in methane have been replaced.  Thus, OH, Cl, Br and COOH are substituents .  Among the substituents, one of them is considered as  the main or principal   substituent.  It will represent the main functional group suffix while  the rest are treated as prefixes.  In the above example, if COOH is considered as the  main constituent, then, OH, Br and Cl will be treated as  prefixes.  ALKENES AND ALKYNES HAVE VACAN T POSITIONS .  Alkenes have two vacant positions while alkynes  have four vacant positions. They are not filled.  Therefore, they are unsaturated hydrocarbons.  NUMENCLATURE  Alkane = C n H 2n+2   SP 3  Alkene = alkane   - 2H= C n H 2n   SP 2  ALKYNE = alkane   - 4H= C n H 2n - 2   SP  SP 3   is the farthest from the nucleus while the SP is  the closest.SP form more stronger bonds  NOTE ON ALKENE  [C n H 2n+2 ]   -   2H=   C n H 2n  It has an hybridization of   SP 2  This means, there are two vacant positions in an  alkene. There is always a double bond in an alkene to  show these vacant positions.  Unlike alkanes , a single carbon   atom   cannot carry a  double bond.   Two carbon atoms are needed. This is  why alkene begins wi th C 2   .  While there is METHANE in an alkane, there is no  METHENE .  So an alkene   has   two carbon atoms carrying a double  bond.  Instead of one carbon atom losing two hydrogen  atoms, the loss is shared between the two carbon  atoms.   Thus, each carbon   atom   with the double  bond loses   a   hydrogen atom. Or better still,   each  carbon with double bond has a vacant position .

HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional   chemistry material you probably have not read!   408  Alkene does not undergo substitution reactions.  As you can see, it still needs more. It has vacant  positions. Thu s an alkene undergoes   addition  reaction. And once the two positions are filled, it  becomes saturated or an alkane.  Like alkenes, an alkyne does not undergo  substitution reaction. As you can see, it has vacant  four positions.  Thus an alkyne undergoes additional reaction.  A nd once the four positions are filled, it becomes  saturated or an alkane.  It is important to note that alkynes are twice  unsaturated as alkenes.  Alkenes for example, needs one hydrogen  molecule(H 2 ) to become saturated while alkynes  needs two molecules of   hydrogen(2H 2 ).  THE ALKYL   GROUP  DEFINITION  Alkyl   includes all groups derived from alkanes by  the loss of a hydrogen atom.  ALKANE minus one hydrogen atom equals an ALKYL  CnH 2n + 2   minus one H atom = Alkyl.  Alkane   = C n H 2n + 2  Alkyl   = C n H 2n + 2   –   1   = C n H 2n + 1     The alkyl is represented with   R     When you change the ‘ ane ’ in alkane to ‘ yl ’, you  will have the alkyl     For example  Methane   –   CH 4   and   Ethane   –   C 2 H 6  If one hydrogen is removed from each compound,  above, you wil l get an alkyl  Methyl   –   CH 3  Ethyl   –   C 2   H 5  NOTE ON ALKYNE  [C n H 2n+2 ]   -   4 H=   C n H 2n - 2  It has an hybridization of SP  This means, there are   four vacant positions in an  alky ne.  There is always a triple bond in an alkyne to show  these vacant positions.  Like alkenes , a single carbon cannot carry a triple  bond.   Two carbon atoms are needed. This is why an  alky ne also begins with   C 2   just like alkenes.  Thus,w hile there is METHANE in a n alkane, there is  no METHYNE .  So an alkyne has two carbon atoms carrying a  triple bond.  Instead of one carbon atom losing four hydrogen  atoms, the loss is shared between the two carbon  atoms.  Thus, each carbon atom with the triple   bond   loses  twp   hydroge n atom s . Or better still ,   each carbon  with triple bond has two vacant positions .

XI.   Methyl   CH 3.  XII.   Ethyl   C 2 H 5.  XIII.   Propyl   C 3 H 7.  XIV.   Butyl   C 4 H 9.  XV.   Pentyl   C 5   H 11.  XVI.   Hex yl   C 6 H 13.  XVII.   Heptyl   C 7 H 15.  XVIII. THE FUNCTIONAL GROUP  DEFINATION  The   functional group is an atom ,   a radical  (group of atoms) or a bond common to a  homologus series which determines the main  chemical properties of the series.  NOTE     H ydrocarbons   consist of carbon and hydrogen  only.     They   are generally not very reactive.     Again, the alkyl group being an hydrocarbon,  supports all the general properties of covalent  compounds     More so ,   w hen one hydrogen atom is removed  from   an alkane, what happens? Yes?  An alkyl is formed!     A fter the hydrogen is removed from   an   alkane,  its posi tion is not left vacant .     This means,   another substance must take the  position of the lost hydrogen.     Thus, whatever replaces the lost hydrogen in  an alkane is called   a functional group .  Functional Groups include:  :  COOH,COO,CONH2,NH2,CO,COH , etc.

ETHANE - METHANE=CH 2  PROPENE - ETHENE=CH 2  BUTYNE - PROPYNE=CH 2  CH 2 = 12+2=14  HOMLOGOUS SERIES   =  ALKYL GROUP +   FUNCTIONAL GROUP  ALKYL + OH   = ALKANOL  ALKYL + COOH   = ALKANOIC ACID  ALKYL + COOR   ’   = ALKANOATE OR ESTER  ALKYL + COH   =   ALKANAL  ALKYL + CO   =   ALKANONE  ALKYL + CONH 2   =   AMIDE  ALKYL + NH 2   =   AMINE  SUMMARY

Any other substance that replaces hydrogen in any of  the four positions is a called substituents  Br, OH, COOH and Cl are all substituents .  They replaced hydrogen methane.  Among the substituents, one of them will be the  suffix or the principal   substituent while the others  will form the prefix es.  So most constituents have two names -   one as  prefix and the other as suffix.     OH is ‘OL’ as suffix while it is ‘HYDROXL’  as prefix     The halogens cannot act as suffixes.  They only have names as prefix.     Double and triple bonds cannot act as  prefixes. They only have names as suffix  CASE 1     If   we make ‘ COOH   ‘ the functional  group,  The compound above becomes:  3 - Bromo , 2 - Chloro, 3 -   Hydroxyl, Propan - 1 - oic  acid  If the carbon in ‘COOH’ is not added, then it  becomes  Or  2 - Bromo , 1 - Chloro, 2 -   Hydroxyl,   C arboxylic acid  When the carbon position is   one , it is usually  removed. So the name becomes :     3 - Bromo , 2 - Chloro, 3 -   Hydroxyl,  Propanoic acid  or     2 - Bromo , Chloro,   2 - Hydroxyl   Carboxylic  acid  CASE   2  If we make ‘OH ‘ the functional group,  then the name changes to:     Bromo , 2 - carboxyl ,   2 - Chloro Ethanol

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!   438  INTRODUCTION TO CHEMISTRY  Chemistry is a pure science which studies the composition, the properties and the   composition of  matter.  The key words from the definition above include:  Pure science  Properties  Composition of matter  Science is an organized body of knowledge. In other words, science deals with facts.  Facts are provable. Facts have evidences.  According   to science water freezes at 0 0 C   and boils at 100 0 C . It is so everywhere in the world.  It has been proven all over the wrong. Therefore, it is a scientist fact.  Every scientific fact begins with observation and hypothesis.  Observations are what we see, h ear, feel, smell or taste.  Hypothesis is what we think based on our observations.  Hypothesis needs experiment to prove whether they are right or wrong.  When supported by an experiment, it becomes a theory or   a law.  There are three pure science  - 1 -   Biology   which is a study of life  - 2 -   Physics which studies matter in relation to e nergy. Physicist are more interes ted in energy  - 3 - Chemistry.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!   439  Matter is anything that has mass or weight and occupies space  There is a relationship between mass and weight  Weight =   Mass x acceleration due to gravity  Mathematically,   W   = mg  The acceleration due gravity is inversely proportional to the radius of the earth .   ( 𝑔   𝛼   1  𝑟 2   )   .  This means as radius increases, the acceleration due to gravity reduces.  The is why acceleration due to gravity is highest at the   N orth and   S outh p oles while it is lowest at  the E quator  STATES OF MATTER  There are 3 states or forms of matter: solid , liquid and gas  COMPOSITION OF MATTER  There are 3 building blocks of matter .   They are known as the composition of matter  1.   Atom  2.   molecule  3.   A nd ion  1.   An atom is the smallest particle   of an element which can take part in a chemical reaction.  Key note     An atom is not the smallest particle of an element.  This is because we have particles   smaller than an atom such as proton, electron and  neutron. They are called sub - atomic particles.     Howeve r in chemical reactions, proton , neutron and electron are too small.  So for chemical reactions,   an atom is the smallest.  An atom can also be defined as   the smallest particle of an element which can exist  and still retain   all   the properties that   element .  2.   A molecule= atom + atom  A molecule is the smallest part of a substance which can exist alone and still retain all the  properties of that substance be it   an element or a compound.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!   440  There are two types of molecule  a.   Molecule of an element  b.   Molecule of a compound  In molecule of an element no new substance is formed :   H   +   H   →   H 2  However in molecule of a compound a new substance is always formed :   Na + Cl   →   NaCl  What is atomicity?  Atomicity is the number of atoms   in a   molecule  ATOMICITY   ATOMS   EXAMPLES  Monatomic molecule   1   Noble gases  Diatomic molecule   2   Halogens, N 2 ,O 2 ,H 2  Triatomic molecule   3   OZONE (O 3 )  Polyatomic molecule   More than three  Phosphorus has 4  atoms(triatomic)  Sulphur has   8  atoms. (octatomic)  The noble gases are:  Helium , Neon, A rgon etc  The halogens are:  Flourine , Chlorine, Bromine and I odine

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!   442  PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL CHANGE  1.   PHYSICAL CHANGE  A physical change is easily reversible and no new substance is formed .  Examples  Magnetization  Melting of candle wax  Change of state e.g. freezing melting,   evaporation etc.  2.   CHEMICAL CHANGE  It is a change which is not easily reversible and a new substance is always of formed.  Examples  - burning of substance  - corrosion of metals eg the rusting of iron  - fermentation of palm wine to alcohol  - decay of substance  - addition of water to quicklime  CaO   +   H 2 O   →   Ca(OH) 2  q uick lime   water   lime water     Chemical change involves the evolution of heat and   can   be represente d with   chemical  equations unlike physical change .

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!   443  ELEMENT, COMPOUND AND MIXTURE  1.   An element is a substance which cannot be split by ordinary chemical reactions  Note  There are   two   types of reaction: chemical reactions and nuclear reactions .     Chemical reactions involve transfer of electrons and the element is not destroyed in the  process.     Nuclear reactions , however,   involve the nucleus   and   the element is destroyed   in the  process.  Nuclear reactions evolve or give   out a lot of heat.  2.   A compound is a chemical combination of element s .  Compounds are   formed by chemical bonding . It is a chemical change  3.   Mixture involve physical change which is a combination of constituents whi ch can be  separated   by   physical means or separation techniques  NOTE  Sometimes the process is not reversible at all e.g. when you burn your uniform while ironing it.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!   444  SEPARATION TECHIQUES  There are different methods   employ ed   to separate the components of mixture.  1.   Separation techniques that use method of boiling point  - evaporation ,   simple distillation   an   fractional distillation  The three   of   them involve miscible liquids.  Two separation techniques are used for reco very of salt s  - 1 -   evaporation to dryness if the salt does not decomposed on heating  - 2 -   crystallization if the salt decomposes on heating  Crystallization is used in industries where purity is of uttermost importance.  It is used in drugs and sugar producti on .  There are   ways of inducing crystal formation .  By addition of crystal salt or seeding and by scratching the side of the vessel.  Crystallization is specially employed in pharmaceutical industries where drugs are produced.  Simple distillation and   fractional distillation  - For   mixture of two miscible liquids , simple distillation is used if their boiling point difference is  wide, if not fractional distillation is used.  If the com ponents are   more than two liquids, fractional distillation is used.  The   main difference between simple distillation and fractional distillation is  FRACTIONATING COLUMN .  This is   why   fractional distillation can separate more than two miscible liquids.  Fractional distillation   is employed in the s eparation   of petroleum or crude   oil.  - Both simple and fractional distillation have   LIEBIG CONDENSER   which convert s   vapour to  distillate  SOLUBILITY  - Separation techniques like chromatography, precipitation, separating funnel have something to  do with solubility.  - Among all the separation   chromatography is   one of   the purest.   This is   why   it   is   used in  industries where purity is of uttermost importance.   I t is widely used in food and breweries  industries.  - It also used in pharmaceutical industries to   produce   drug s .

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!   445  There three types of   chromatography  1.   Paper chromatography. I t is the commonest  2.   Gas  3.   Column  Chromatography is used in separating the components of   dye,   ink and chlorophyll in plants .  It can also be used to analyze polluted water or air, blood and urine in medical laboratory, as well  as the components of crude oil.  Paper chromatography is used to identify the components of protein  Other separation techniques include :  Sieve : is used in   garri making industries to separate particles of different sizes  Filtration : is   widely used in water treatment   plant .  It is used a lot in qu alitative analysis.   It is used to separate   two   immiscible mixture.  Other separation used in separating two   immiscible liquids are   sedimentation and  decantation .  Sublimation   is   used for solid substance which   go es   directly to gas without melting to liquid.  Examples are iodine crystal, ammonium salts, naphthalene ,dry ice or solid  carbon(IV) oxide   etc.  To test fo r the purity of a substance, we either check its boiling point or melting point.  A pure substance will have sharp boiling or melting points.  It will also have definite relative density and definite refractive index.  Generally, impurities lowers melting p oint and raises boiling points of liquid substances .  Sometimes   dirt   in   wat er is allowed to sediment or sett le before separating them by decantation  - In evaporation the solvent   or liquid is lost or sacrificed while in simple and fractional distillation,  the   solvent is recovered.  Among all the separation,   Precipitation   involve s a chemical change.  Note air is a mixture for 4 reasons.   Check page………………………..  Fractional crystallization   :  This method is used to separate two or more solids which are present in the   same solution in  roughly equal amounts. Their solubility usually differs at different temperatures. This makes one  salt crystallizes out first while the other crystallizes at a later temperature.  Centrifugation:   It uses a centrifuge machine to separate plasma from blood cells.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  448  ATOMIC STRUCTURE   1  JOHN DALTON’S THEORY  1.   All elements are made up of small, indivisible particle called   ATOMS.  2.   Atoms can neither be created nor destroyed.  3.   Atoms of the same element are alike in all aspects and differ from atoms of every  other element.  4.   When atoms combine, they do so in a small whole ratio.  5.   Chemical reactions results from the combination or   separation of atoms.  ADVANTAGES OF DALTON’S THEORY  1.   Element were represented with symbols. e.g. Mg, H, O, Na  2.   Compounds were represented with formulae. e.g. H 2 O  3.   Chemical reactions were represented with equations. e.g. 2H 2   + O 2   2H 2 O  DISADVANTAGE  1.   John Dalton’s T heories could not explain the formation of ion or electrolysis.  MODIFICATION TO JOHN DALTON’S THEORY  1.   The discover y of the sub - atomic particles ( protons, Neutron &   electrons )   shows  that an atom is divisible.  2.   The study of radio activity or   nuclear chemistry reveals that an atom can be  destroyed.  3.   The phenomenon of Isotopy shows that the atoms of the same element can be  different.  4.   Lastly, except for ordinary reaction reactions, atoms can be combine in thousands  in   organic chemistry .  LAWS THAT   SUPPORTED JOHN DALTON’S THEORY.     The law of the conservation of matter     The law of definite proportion     The law of multiple proportion     The law of the reciprocal proportion

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  449  1.   law   of the conservation of matter:  This states that matter can neither be created   nor destroyed but can be converted  from one form to another.  2.   law of definite proportion:  This states that all pure sample of a particular compound contains the same  element combined in the same proportions by mass.  3.   law of multiple proportion:  This states   that if two element A and B combine chemically together to form more  than one various masses of element A which combine separately with a fixed  mass of element B are in simple multiple ratio   .  NOTE  -   According Rutherford,   the atom has a dense centre where   the protons   and   the  n eutron are concentrated.  -   He also suggested that electrons move round the   n ucleus

There are smaller particles called the sub -   atomic particles  -  Facts from the table above  -   An atom is Neutral  -   WHY?  -   Because it contains equal number of proton and electron  -   The nucleus of every element is positively changed.  -   WHY?  -   Because, they contain a positively charged particle called   proton.  -   The proton and the neutron are 1,840 times heavier than the mass of the  electron.  -   In other words, the mass of the electron is 1,840 times less than the mass of  the proton or neutron.  Note  The only condition whereby gases conduct electricity is when pressure is decreased  and voltage is increased.  The charge carriers of   g ases are electron   and   ion.  The charge carriers of semi conducts are electrons   and   holes.  The charge carriers in electrolyte are ions.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  451  ATOMS AND IONS  -   Atom is formed when proton number is equal to electron number.  -   When the proton number is not equal to an electron number an ion is formed.  -   The charge of an atom is zero or   neutral.  -   When an atom carries a positive or negative charge, it is no longer an atom.  -   An ion , therefore, is defined as an atom or group of atoms which possesses  charge.  Question  What is responsible for the formation of an ion and why?  Answer  Change in electron number  -   - Reason  -   Proton number never changes.  -   Electrons can be gained or lost.  For example  𝑁𝑎 +   ,   𝑀𝑔 2 +   ,   𝐴𝑙 3 +   show that electron (s)   have been lost.   How?  -   The plus sign on top of each of the atoms above show s   that the proton number is  greater than the electron number.  -   And since proton number never changes. This implies that electron has been lost.  -   𝐶𝑙 −   ,   𝑂 2 −   ,   𝑆 2 −   reveal that the electron number is greater than the proton number.  -   And since proton number does not change. This implie s that electron s   must have  been gained.     Negative ions mean that electrons have been gained.  Electrons are negative in nature.  𝐶𝑙   +   𝑒 −   →   𝐶𝑙 −   (f rom   0   to   - 1… that is reduction )  𝑂   +   2 𝑒 −   →   𝑂 2 −   …that is reduction  The more electron s   an atom gains, the more negative   value   it will   have . Thus, atoms  that ionize by electron gain undergo reduction.     Positive ions mean that electrons have been lost.  Electrons are negative in nature.  𝑁𝑎   −   𝑒 −   →   𝑁𝑎 +   (from 0 to +1…that is oxidation)  𝑀𝑔   −   2 𝑒 −   →   𝑀𝑔 2 +  𝐴𝑙   −   3 𝑒 −   →   𝐴𝑙 3 +  The more electron s   an atom loses, the more positive   value it will have .  Thus, atoms that ionize by electron loss undergo oxidation.(or increment)

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  452  Question  Atomic number is a basic property of all elements .WHY?  -   This is b ecause different elements have different atomic number s .  -   In other words, no two different elements can have the same atomic number.  Note  -   Different elements can have the same phy sical and chemical properties, b ut they  cannot have the same atomic number.  -   Sodium is the only element with atomic number 11  -   Chlorine is the element with atomic number 17.  -   Atomic number is the only property of an element which  distinguishes it from every   other element.  In fact, the atomic number is used to determine the chemical properties of all  elements.  DEFINITION  1.   Atomic number is the number of proton .This is used for both atoms and  ions.  2.   Atomic number is the number of electron in an   ATOM . This is   used for  ATOMS only  Remember that in an atom, proton number and electron number are  equal.  This is why an atom is a neutral particle.  Question  Why is atomic number usually defined ,   as the number of proton.  Answer  Proton number does not change.  ATOMIC   MASS.  1.   ATOMIC MASS   is the sum of proton number and neutron number. This is  used for both atoms and ions.  2.   ATOMIC MASS   is also the sum of electron number and neutron number   in an  ATOM .  This is used for ATOMS only  Remember that in an atom , proton number and   electron number are equal. This is  why an atom is a neutral particle. They have the same atomic number or proton number .  Isotopes hav e different physical properties.  QUESTION  Why is it that the relative atomic masses of elements are not usually whole number? ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  458  ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATION (E.C.)  This is the arrangement of electrons in shell. The shells are K, L, M , N OR 1,2,3,4 etc.  Another name for shells are PERIODS  So period 1 = K shell  Period 2 = L shell  The shells are further divided into   sub - shells : s   p   d   f  Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in shells in the ascending order of  their energy levels.  1s 2   2s 2   2p 6   3s 2   3p 6   4s 2   3d 10 , 4p 6  - Every element with a completely filled shell is placed in group zero or eight.  This why the first period contains two elements only.  They are Hydrogen in group 1 and Helium in group 8.  Why is Helium placed in group 8 and not group 2?  This is because it completes the K - SHELL. In other words,  its shell is filled up. And elements   with filled up shells are placed in group 8.  Why are there only two elements in period 1?  This is because K - shell can only take maximum of 2 electrons.  Thus, Helium is the only noble gas with a duplet structure. The others have octet structures.  Duplet m eans 2 while octet means 8  Using 2n 2 , we can determine the number of electrons in a shell  K or 1   2n 2   = 2(1) 2   =2 x1 = 2   S 2  L or 2   2n 2   = 2(2) 2   =2 x4 = 8   S 2   p 6  M or 3   2n 2   = 2(3) 2   =2 x9 = 18   S 2   p 6   d 10  N or 4   2n 2   = 2(4) 2   =2 x16 = 32   S 2   p 6   d 10   f 14  If s - orbital takes 2 electrons, if you add 4, you will get p=6. If you add 4  again, you will d=10 and add another 4, you will get f=14

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  468  Bonding or chemical combination is the ‘marriage’ of elements to form molecules.  Types of bondings  1.   Ionic or   electrovalent bond which involves a metal and a non -   metal.  2.   Ordinary covalent bond shall be treated as covalent bond  3.   Dative bond or coordinate covalent bond

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  469  IONIC OR ELECTROVALENT BOND  Electrovalent bond is a bond that exists between a metal and a   non - metal in which the  metal donates its outer most electron (s)   to the non -   metal so that both of them can attain a  duplet or an octet structure or configuration like the noble gases.  There is a complete transfer of electron (s)   from the metal to the non - me tal.  The more the electronegative difference between a metal and a non - metal, the stronger will  be the ionic bond formed between them.  The electronegative difference can be related to the distance between the two elements in  the periodic table.  For instan ce, the distance between group 1 and 7 elements is wider than any other groups.  This means, the electronegative difference between group 1 and group 7 is the highest.  Therefore, ionic bond between group 1 and group 7 will be the strongest.  Examples of   ionic compounds  Example 1

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  470  Example 2: MgCl 2  Example 3: AlCl 3

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  471

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  472  Example 4: Al 2 O 3  2Al= 2x3=6 electrons  3 O= 3X2= 6 electrons  One atom of aluminum has 3 electrons to give out   while one oxygen atom needs 2  electrons.  If aluminum gives out 2electrons, one electron will be left.  So in order for both of them to become ions, we have to multiply aluminum   atom   by  what oxygen needs and multiply oxygen by what al uminum can give:   [2Al   3O].  Example 5: CaO

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  473  COVALENT BOND  Covalent bond: is a bond between two non - metals .Sharing is involved in covalent   bond.  Definition  Covalent bond is a bond that exists between two non -   metals in which both of them  contribute electrons equally and share them equally in order for both of them to attain a  duplet or an octet structure or configuration like the noble gases.  Example 1: H 2  Example 2: Cl 2  Example 3: HCl

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  474  Example 4: H 2 O (water)  Example : NH 3   (Ammonia)  Example 5: CH 4

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  475  DATIVE OR CO - ORDINATE COVALENT BOND  Dative bond is a special type of covalent bond which tends to make a covalent molecule   to  be less volatile.  For Dative bond to occur, one of the participants must have at least one lone pair of  electrons to be shared.  A lone pair is two electrons which are together in its orbital.  Examples of lone pairs  1.   Carbon has no lone pairs.   3.  2.   4 .  water has 2 lone pair and 2 shared pair

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  476  DEFINITION  Dative bond is a bond in one of the participants donates the electrons which are shared, so  that both of them can attain a duplet or an octet   structure or configuration like the noble  gases.  Examples include: formation of complex salts, ammonium ion (NH 4 + ), ozonium ions  (H 3 O + ).  Example 1  Example 2  differences between ionic and covalent compounds  IONIC COMPOUNDS   COVALENT COMPOUND  -   They are held by electrostatic  force of attraction  They are held by inter - molecular forces  -   They form ions.   They form molecules  -   They dissolve in polar solvent  e.g .,   water  They dissolve in non - polar or organic  solvents e.g ., b enzene, ether  -   They are good electrolytes in  solution i.e .,   they can conduct  electricity  They are non -   electrolyte  -   They have high melting and  boiling point  They have low melting and boiling  point.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  477  INTERMOLECULAR FORCES  There are three types  1.   Hydrogen bond  2.   Vander Waals  3.   Permanent induced dipole  These are the forces which are responsible for covalent compounds.  Generally, covalent compounds do not dissolve in polar solvent like water.  However, covalent compounds like CH 3 Cl, CHCl 3 , H 2 S, NH 3   , HCl dissolve in water. Why?  NOTE  In covalent bonding, we assume the electrons are equally shared but in reality, that is   not  always the case.  The electronegative strength of the elements actually determ in es how the electrons are  shared. If the elements have equal or almost equal electronegative strength, the electron will  be equally shared.  In such case, the covalent compo und formed will exhibit all the properties of covalent  compounds.  The intermolecular which supports all the covalent properties is the van der waal forces.  However, if electrons are not equally shared, the shape of the covalent molecule will be  disfigur ed or distorted. And whenever that happens, the covalent compound will be polar or  soluble in water.  This is what happens with hydrogen bond and permanent induced dipole.  1.   HYDROGEN BOND  This happens when hydrogen goes into covalent bond with highly   electronegative elements  like oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and the halogens(F 2 ,Cl 2 , Br 2 , I 2 ).  Definitely the electrons will not be equally shared and that will distort or disfigure the shape  of the molecule. Covalent compounds with hydrogen bond are polar or   soluble in water .  E xamples include, alkanol, alkanoic acid, HCl, H 2 S, NH 3   etc.  Non -   metallic properties decrease down the group. That means, electronegativity of the  halogen decrease s   from F 2   to I 2   .  F 2   Cl 2   Br 2   I 2  Electronegativity d ecreases  Fluorine is the most electronegative non - metal. This means hydrogen bold decreases with  halogen down the group. Hydrogen iodide is the least soluble in that group.  Effects of hydrogen bonding  1.   It makes a covalent compound polar   (or dissolve in water).  2.   It makes a covalent compound to have high melting and boiling points  3.   It leads to the formation of aggregates e.g. HF…..H 2 F 2 …H 3 F 3

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  479  VAN DER WAALS AND PERMANENT   INDUCED DIPOLE  Identify the intermolecular force   in each of the following with a reason and  give another example like the one identified.  Answer:   V an der waals  Reason:   the shape is not distorted because  the force of hydrogen on carbon is the same  in all the four directions.  Another example like the above is  tetrachloromethane  The effect of chlorine on carbon in all  the four directions is same.  They will exhibit all covalent  properties.  This means, they will not dissolve in  water.  Answer:   Permanent induced dipole  Reason:   the shape will be distorted  because chlorine is more electronegative  than hydrogen.  Another example like the above is  trichloromethane  They will therefore, dissolve in water

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  481  METALLIC   BOND  Metallic bond holds atoms of a metal in its crystal lattice.  It has a pool where each atom donates its valence electron.  When that happens, the atoms become positively charged while the electron cloud becomes  negatively charged. This will   then set up an electrostatic force of attraction known as  metallic bond. Metals with higher valence electrons like Magnesium and aluminum form  stronger metallic bond. This is why metallic bond increases across the period and atomic  size decreases.  NOTE  Van der waals holds atoms of non -   metals noble gases in their crystal lattice.  As the number of electrons increases, the van der waals increases.  This is why van der increases down the group.  In group 7 for instance, as we g o down the group,   fluorine and c hlorine are gases, bromine  is liquid while iodine is a volatile solid. ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  484  MOLECULAR FORMULA AND EMPIRICAL FORMULA  MOLECULAR FORMULA  Molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element that combine to  form a compound.  Examples  C 6 H 12 O 6 ,   H 2 SO 4 , CaCO 3,   C 12 H 22 O 11  note :   ( glucose   ×   2 )   −   1H 2 O   =   sucrose  =   2 (   C 6 H 12   O 6 )   −   1H 2 O   =   C 12 H 24 O 12   −   H 2 O  sucrose   =   C 12 H 22   O 11  EMPIRICAL FORMULA  Empirical formula gives the simplest ratio of atoms that combine to give a  compound.  It can also be called the simplest formula.  The molecular formula of glucose and fructose is   the same.   ( C 6 H 12 O 6 )  Let us divide through by 6  C 6 H 12 O 6  6   =   CH 2 O     CH 2 O   is   the   simplest   formula   of   glucose .   It   is   the   empirical   of   glucose .  Ethene has a molecular formula   C 2 H 4  If we divide through by 2, its empirical formula becomes  C 2 H 4  2   =   CH 2  Empirical   formula is called the simplest formula.  NOTE     Sometimes, the empirica formula of a particular compound and its molecular  formula may be the same e.g. H 2 O.  At some other time, they may be different e.g. reducing sugar (glucose).  Reducing sugar e.g. glucose and fructose. Both of them are monosaccharide. They  have the same molecular formula [   C 6 H 12 O 6 )].  In organic chemistry, they are described as isomers.  NOTE     If the empirical formula is different from the molecular formula, we wi ll use the  empirical formula mass and the RMM of the compound to calculate the molecular  formula.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  507  KINETIC THEORY   OF GASES  1.   Gas molecules consist of small molecules which move randomly in straight  lines.  2.   The molecules are perfectly elastic and possess kinetic energy. Hence they are  moving randomly colliding with one another and the walls of the containing  vessels as su ch exerting pressure. Energy is not lost during collision but can  only be transformed to another form.  3.   The intermolecular forces are negligible and molecules appear to be  independent of one another.  4.   The size of the molecules are so small and far apart that   the gas occupied a  negligible volume   compared with that of the container.  5.   The temperature of the gas is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the  gas particles.  NOTE  Diffusion is the movement of particles from region of higher concentration through a  porous medium to a region of lower concentration. It is fastest in gases than in solid  and liquid.  When the moving particle is water, then it is called osmosis. In osmosis, the water  moves from higher concentration to a region of lower concentration throu gh semi -  permeable membrane.  Effusion is the movement of particles of matter or gases through a small aperture  under pressure.  Brownian movement which involves zig   - zag or irregular movements of particles,  diffusion and osmosis support kinetic theory.  BOYLE’S LAW  Boyle’s law states that the volume of a given mass of a gas is inversely  proportional to the pressure at constant temperature  V α   1  P  V   =   k  P  k   =   VP  V 1 P 1   =   V 2 P 2  Examples

GAY LUSSAC’S LAW  When gases react, they do so in volume which are in simple ratio to one  another and to the volume of the produc t if gaseous, provided temperature  and pressure remain constant.  Mole= volume…………..according to   Gay Lussac  Volume= molecule……….according to Avogadro  Therefore in calculations of Gay Lussac, moles in equation will be changed to  volume. ,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  530  THE PERIODIC TABLE   2  This is the arrangement of element in groups and period according to their  atomic numbers.  -   There are 8, groups and 7 period in a   periodic table  -   Electrons revolve around the Nucleus in spherical region called shells or  energy levels which are situated at various distance from the Nucleus  -   The radius of each shell from the Nucleus is always specific.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  531  In chemistry, there are different ways of saying the same thing.  It is important that you know some of them so that you do not get unnecessarily  confused.  For example  The opposite of least   = most  The opposite of metallic = non metallic  Therefore,  Most metallic   can be expressed as   least non metallic  Least non -   metallic can be expressed as most metallic  Let us examine the table again

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  532  Least electronegative=most electropositive  Most elect ropositive=least electronegative  Most oxidizing=least reducing  Most reducing=least oxidizing  Oxidation or Oxidized= metal  Most oxidized= most metallic  Least oxidized= least metallic  Reduction or reduced= non metals  Most reduced= most non - metallic  Least   reduced= least non - metallic  PERIODIC LAW  -   States that the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic  numbers.  Periodic means occurring at regular intervals   .  -   Function means depends on  The law above suggests that when elements are   arranged in increasing order of  their atomic numbers, there is a regular repetition of their properties from 1 to  group 8 .  This explains why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.  Sodium and potassium are in group 1. Therefore, they   share similar chemical  properties.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  533  The only reason for this is because the properties of elements repeats themselves  in periods which is determined by their atomic number.  Atomic number is a basic property of every element. It is basically the only  prope rty which distinguishes elements. This is because no two different elements  have the same atomic number. They may have some chemical and physical  resemblance but they cannot have the same atomic number except they are  isotopes of the same element.  PERIODI CITY  These are properties of elements which increase or decrease across the period or  down the groups.  -   In relation to periodic table, periodicity is the variation of the properties of  element in regular patterns in groups and across the periods.  Example of periodicity     Atomic size and atomic radius     Electropositivity   and e lectronegativity     Ionic radius and ionic size     IONIZATION ENERGY  FOUR FACTORS AFFECT THE PERIODICITY OF ELEMENT  i).   Number of valence electron (or outermost electrons)  ii).   Nuclear charge  iii).   Screening effect of inner electrons  iv).   Numbers of shells  These four factors are basically two factors because nuclear charge  and screening effect of inner electrons are consequences of the  other two factors.  For example  1.   Number of outermost   electrons increases nuclear charge  2.   Number of shells increases screening effect of inner electrons  -   The number of shells and the outermost electrons (or valence electrons)  cannot increase at the same time. If one increases, the other will be constant  and vi ce versa.  NOTE  -   Nuclear charge is the charge of the nucleus. It is positively charged because  the nucleus contains protons.

,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,, HINTS ON CHEMISTRY PRACTICALS  An exceptional chemistry material you probably have not   read!  534  -   Nuclear charge always brings about attraction. ‘It tends to bring together’  -   Screening effect of inner electrons, on the ot her hand, is negatively charged.  -   It always brings about repulsion. In other words, ‘It tends to ‘scatter’  Across the period, the number of outermost electrons increases while the  number of shells remains the same.  As a result, the nuclear charge which t ends to bring together (or the force of  attraction) prevails over screening effect of inner electrons.  Consequently, atomic size will reduce and ionization energy will increase  across the period.  Even metallic bond increases as the outermost electrons inc reases across the  period.  Increase in nuclear charge favours non - metals. Thus, non   - metallic  properties increase across the period.  On the other hand, down the group, the number of shells increases while the  outermost electrons remain the same.  As a resu lt , the screening effect which tends to scatter (or the force of  repulsion) prevails over the nuclear charge.  Consequently, atomic size increases while ionization energy decreases down  the group.  Increase in screening effect of inner electrons favours   metals. Thus, metallic  properties increase down the group.  Note: Metallic bond decreases down the group .  IONIZATION ENERGY     This is the amount of energy required to remove an electron(S) from the outer  most shell of an element or an atom to become an ion     I t is a property of metals since metals ionize by electron loss.     High reactive metals have low ionization energy values     It increases across the period but decreases down the group.  ELECTRON AFFINITY  This is the amount of energy release d when an electron(s) are added to the  outer most shell of an atom to become an ion.     It is directly opposite to ionization energy.     It is a property of non - metal since they ionize by electron gain     It decreases across the period but increase down the group  ELERCTRONEGATIVITY     This is the power of an element to attracts electron to itself e.g. Chlorine is more  electronegativity than sodium because it is easily gained an electron to become  an ion     It increases across the period but decreas es down the group  ATOMIC RADIUS

ATOMIC SIZE  This is the distance between the nuclei or center of two covalently bonded atom.     Both atomic size and atomic radius decrease across the period but increase down  the group  QUESTION  Why is it   that the ionic radius of the non - metals is always bigger than that of the  metal positively?  ANSWER  Because metals lose their outermost shell whenever they ionize.  IONIC RADIUS  This is the half of the distance between the nuclei of   two covalently bonded ions.
